text:
Diesel Relief, Deeper Risks | October 10, 2026
(📍Data From https://t.co/rtKhA53pFF Daily Report)

Washington is seeking cheaper fuel. Households are reporting weaker economic conditions. Inflation expectations are rising again.

That combination deserves more attention than a simple “energy relief is bullish” headline. Additional diesel could ease one pressure point without repairing consumer demand—or restoring confidence in monetary policy.

1️⃣ Consumers feel worse, but expect higher prices

Preliminary October consumer sentiment fell to 46.3 from 48.1. Current economic conditions dropped to 44.7, a record low. One-year inflation expectations rose to 4.7%, while longer-run expectations increased to 3.5%. Importantly, the consumer expectations subindex improved slightly: the deterioration was concentrated in perceptions of current conditions.

My reading: households are struggling with affordability, not simply becoming uniformly pessimistic about the future.

This complicates the policy outlook. Weak sentiment can signal spending pressure, but rising inflation expectations make an easy monetary response harder to justify. The survey alone proves neither recession nor an imminent policy move. Watch actual spending, employment and inflation for confirmation.

2️⃣ Apple offers a company-level demand warning

Apple reportedly reduced October component orders for iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max by at least 15% versus original requests, with higher memory costs and device prices weighing on demand. This concerns specific component orders—not a confirmed equivalent decline in total iPhone revenue.

The trading implication is the cost-versus-volume dilemma. Absorbing expensive components pressures margins; passing costs through risks fewer purchases. If order cuts persist beyond October or promotions intensify, the issue becomes more consequential for earnings estimates.

A premium product does not have unlimited pricing power.

3️⃣ Russian diesel: an announced supply path, not delivered cargo

The U.S. issued a temporary authorization for Russian-origin diesel transactions, including imports, through April 7, 2027. The announced supply sequence starts above 300,000 tons, followed by 500,000 tons in November and another million afterward. Russian officials also indicated readiness to increase exports as refineries return from maintenance. These remain supply commitments and plans, not verified deliveries.

If incremental cargoes arrive, diesel scarcity premiums could ease, helping freight operators and other diesel-intensive businesses while pressuring refining margins.

But diesel is a refined product. Additional diesel supply does not automatically produce an equivalent fall in crude prices. Watch refinery availability, export loadings, destination markets and diesel crack spreads—the margin between diesel and crude.

4️⃣ Energy cooperation has not established a peace breakthrough

The Kremlin said Putin blamed Ukrainian attacks for undermining an immediate restart of negotiations. That is Moscow’s account, not an independently established explanation. Zelensky criticized the diesel agreement as benefiting Russia.

The market distinction matters: fuel-market cooperation can coexist with continued conflict. Removing some supply restrictions does not eliminate geopolitical risk.

Separately, eight countries’ foreign ministers opposed U.S. sanctions against the International Criminal Court. This adds evidence of diplomatic disagreement, but does not by itself establish a measurable move in equities or currencies.

5️⃣ Institutional credibility and supply security remain watchpoints

The White House memorandum establishing an inquiry into Lisa Cook is dated October 7. The committee will assess alleged grounds for removal; its creation is not a removal decision.

For investors, the potential transmission runs through confidence in central-bank independence and inflation control. A higher required risk premium is a scenario to monitor, not an observed consequence established by this announcement.

India is also developing plans for critical-mineral stockpiles. Any purchasing impact depends on the minerals selected, procurement volumes and timing.

Panama’s major earthquake and aftershocks caused damage, with magnitude estimates subsequently revised. Shipping disruption requires operational confirmation; the earthquake alone does not establish a Panama Canal closure.

Trader’s takeaway: Supply relief would be constructive if it lowers delivered fuel costs without fresh disruptions. The adverse combination is delayed cargoes, persistent inflation expectations and weaker consumer spending.

Cheaper diesel can help. It cannot carry the entire macro outlook.

Same Title, Double the Pay: The Salary Gap Nobody Shows You

This month, Anthropic posted a staff engineering role with a base salary of $405K to $485K. The median for similar roles is about $224K.

That's the same job title with roughly double the pay. And it isn't just frontier AI labs. A typical ML engineer earns somewhere around $170K to $245K in total compensation. At a frontier lab, the same title can pay $600K to over $1M, most of it in equity.

Transparency is coming, but slowly

Since October 1, Connecticut has required every job posting to include a pay range. Sixteen states plus DC now have some kind of pay-transparency law, and Delaware joins in 2027. Across the Atlantic, Denmark just introduced its version of the EU's pay-transparency rules.

That's real progress, but a posted range is wide, and it only tells you what a company plans to pay a future hire. It doesn't tell you what the person sitting next to you makes, what the hiring manager you're about to meet earns, or what a competitor really pays the people you're trying to recruit.

The number that actually matters

When you negotiate an offer, ask for a raise, or hire someone, your leverage comes from knowing the real number. Most people go in blind. Recruiters don't.

That's why we built PayPeek

PayPeek is a Chrome extension that shows estimated pay on any LinkedIn profile, broken into base, equity, bonus, and total compensation, plus how that person's career has progressed. Our estimates usually land within about 7% of verified pay data.

Open a profile, and you'll see the number. It takes one click and no awkward conversations.

Stop guessing

With 2027 raise budgets stuck around 3.5%, waiting for your company to pay you fairly isn't a plan. Knowing your market value is.

A quiet Saturday morning in Las Cruces, New Mexico turned into a horrific nightmare when two armed gunmen shot seven innocent victims - four of them young children - execution-style inside Las Cruces Bowl. 

On the morning of February 10, 1990, the bowling alley was preparing to open its doors. Inside, manager Stephanie Senac was in her office with her 12-year-old daughter, Melissa Repass, and Melissa's friend, 13-year-old Amy Houser. In the kitchen, cook Ida Holguin was starting her day.

As Melissa and Amy were walking to a vending machine, two unidentified men entered through an unlocked door. They pulled out guns and ordered the girls into Stephanie's office. One man approached Holguin, brandishing a .22 caliber pistol, and forced her into the office where the others were gathered. The assailants demanded that everyone lie face down as they emptied the safe, taking between $4,000 to $5,000.

During this ordeal, 26-year-old pin mechanic Steven Teran arrived with his two young daughters, six-year-old Paula Holguin and two-year-old Valerie Teran, intending to drop them off at the alley's daycare. Unaware of the danger inside, they walked into the unfolding nightmare.

The gunmen showed no mercy, shooting all seven victims multiple times at point-blank range. To cover their tracks, they set fire to the office before fleeing the scene.

First responders arrived to a scene of chaos and devastation. Amy Houser, Paula Holguin, and Steven Teran were pronounced dead at the scene. Young Valerie Teran was rushed to the hospital but succumbed to her injuries upon arrival. Remarkably, despite being shot five times, Melissa Repass managed to call 911, a courageous act that brought immediate aid and likely saved lives. Both she and her mother, Stephanie Senac, along with Ida Holguin, survived the attack, though Stephanie later passed away in 1999 due to complications from her injuries.

Police set up multiple roadblocks surrounding Las Cruces quickly after  the shooting, and carefully screened anyone leaving the city. The U.S. Customs Service, Army and Border Patrol searched the area with planes and helicopters. No arrests were ever made. 

One of the witnesses was Stephanie’s brother, Steven, who was at the Las Cruces Bowl just before the murders. He said he had stopped by the bowling alley on his way to school to pick up his backpack. Steven told investigators “I saw two Hispanic gentlemen walking from the back of the building towards the front. The older gentleman handed the younger gentleman a small case. The older gentleman squats down, and looks right at me as I’m driving towards them. I took notice of what they were wearing, and their descriptions, hair color, skin, eyes.” 

During the crime, at some point the suspets tell the victims "this is a hold up" and order Stephanie to open the safe. The men take money from the safe but leave behind additional money that was in there. Ida told police that after the men got into the safe, they began rummaging through all the cabinets as if they were looking for something else other than money.

Las Cruces-Dona Ana County Crime Stoppers continues to offer a $25,000 reward for information that helps identify the men responsible for the mass-shooting. Tips can be provided anonymously by calling Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Tips can also be provided online at https://t.co/Vzp3V9Ij8p or through the Crime Stoppers app, “P3 TIPS.” The app is available through the App Store on most devices.

NEW MOON TONIGHT

“Her Sacred fires are also the fires which burn, and have burned in the past or will burn in future.” 

- Sorita d’Este @theurgia 

🌑 New Moon Ritual to Hekate 🌑

1. Purify the altar with barley, asking to cleanse the space so you can give offerings and speak with respect to the gods.

2. Light a candle and offer a hymn to Hestia. She opens and closes every ritual. (Below is a traditional Orphic Hymn if you so choose.)

"Queen Hestía daughter of mighty Krónos,   
You dwell in the center of the home with your vast everlasting fire,
You purify the initiates of these rites,
Inspire endless youth, wealth, benevolences, and holiness.
You are the dwelling-place of the happy Gods and the strong support of mankind.   
Eternal, many-formed, beloved, and verdant.
Smiling, happy one, accept these offerings with kindness,
Breath upon us wealth and soothing health."

3. Announce yourself. Say “Hekate, hear me.” It’s not a command, just a way of letting her know you’re there to honor her.

4. Speak her ancient titles: Trivia, Savior, Key-holder, of the earth/underworld. Then share what you’ve offered her before, what she’s done for you, and why you’ve come.

5. Invoke her as the one who stands at the crossroads and city gates, bearer of torches, leader of hounds, holder of keys, protector of the home and of children.

6. Say a hymn to Hekate. Here is one based on traditional Ancient Greek translation:

"I call Hekátî of the Crossroads, worshipped at the meeting of three paths, oh lovely one.
In the sky, earth, and sea, you are venerated in your saffron-colored robes.
Funereal Daimôn, celebrating among the souls of those who have passed.
Liminal Mother, fond of deserted places, you delight in deer.
Goddess of night, protectress of dogs, invincible Queen.   
Drawn by a yoke of bulls, you are the queen who holds the keys to all the Kózmos.
Commander, Nýmphi, nurturer of children, you who haunt the mountains.
Pray, Maiden, attend our hallowed rituals;
Be forever gracious to your mystic herdsman and rejoice in our gifts."

7. Make your offerings:
🕯️ Incense, naming anything she’s done for you
🍞 Food, with a small prayer
🍷 A full bottle of wine or grape juice as a libation. Pour one to Hestia first, then Hecate, then close with Hestia again.
8. Pray to Hecate in your own words.
9. Close with Hestia, asking her to tend to those you love and guard the houses of the pious. End with “As the gods will it, so it shall be.”
10. Pour out the container of wine or juice outside. That ends the ritual. ✨

You spent decades in power while your husband turned congressional access into one of the best-performing stock portfolios in America—timed trades around legislation, tech stocks and net worth ballooning from a few million into the hundreds of millions. You blocked or slow-walked serious bans on members trading while the pattern became a national joke. Calling someone else unfit for “dishonoring” the country after that is rich. 
You were Speaker when Nidal Hasan, an Army major, walked into Fort Hood in 2009, shouted “Allahu Akbar,” and killed 13 soldiers and civilians while wounding dozens more. You offered the usual condolences. Republicans on the Intelligence Committee asked for a real look at the intelligence and political-correctness failures that let a radicalized officer keep his access and his weapon. That inquiry didn’t get the urgency the victims’ families deserved. Hasan sat on death row for more than a decade. Now the first military execution in generations is scheduled, by firing squad, at the scene of the crime, and you decide the problem is that Americans might actually watch justice be carried out. 
Hegseth’s stated reason is blunt: people should see that there are serious consequences for an officer who betrays his uniform and massacres his own. Whether livestreaming is wise policy is debatable—plenty of people on both sides find the optics grotesque and worry about martyrdom or recruiting value. But your post doesn’t engage any of that. It just declares him beyond unfit and demands he “must go.” After nearly forty years in the House, two stints as Speaker, two failed impeachments and a party that lost the border, lost working-class voters and watched crime and fentanyl explode under the policies you defended, the “must go” line lands like self-parody. You’re already on the way out in 2027. The electorate has been delivering that message for years.
The same woman who treated the tearing-up of a State of the Union address as theater, who presided over the political weaponization of COVID rules while her own circle enjoyed the usual exemptions and who spent decades as the face of San Francisco governance now lectures a combat veteran about dishonoring the troops. Hasan’s victims were the troops. The spectacle you object to is the public reminder that the man who murdered them is finally scheduled to face the penalty a military court imposed. Your shortfall isn’t subtle: you treat accountability for jihadist murder inside the ranks as the outrage and the people who want consequences as the dishonor. That’s why so many Americans stopped listening to you long before this post.

text:
3/3 This explains the gap between macro measurement and lived experience. The model shows non-cognitive labor compensation rising a relative 11.2% — those physical or on-site service tasks retain scarcity. In reality, displaced knowledge workers cannot transform into scarce skilled tradespeople; they pour into dispatch platforms and gig work. A mass of labor crowding into a fixed market produces what Philip Huang called "involution": longer hours and higher intensity to sustain subsistence, with marginal returns in decline.

The 13.77-million equivalent gap in employment capacity materializes as longer hours, hidden underemployment, and diluted earnings.

The new marginal population has not lost work — they toil day and night, yet they are losing the channel through which work accumulates assets and enables upward mobility. The professional premium is being substituted away; gig backstops sustain subsistence and nothing more. What they face is the practical problem of re-establishing a social position.

VII. Salt and Iron Became Compute; People Must Still Fend for Themselves

For the predicament of ordinary workers seeking self-reliance, history offers a mirror. How a state allocates its core factors — and whether citizens retain room to make independent livings inside a strong-state narrative — was argued head-on in the Discourses on Salt and Iron, two thousand years ago.

Sang Hongyang argued for state command of strategic arteries like salt and iron, concentrating resources for defense and external competition. The Confucian scholars countered that excessive monopoly of the economy's lifelines would squeeze the space for popular self-reliance. The debate posed a question that endures: while concentrating control of resources, how does a state guarantee ordinary people an independent capacity for survival that does not rest on patronage?

Today, compute, models, and data infrastructure are becoming the "new salt and iron" of the intelligent age.

If core factors sit concentrated and centralized actors dominate application scenarios, those pushed out of workstations are left waiting — for uncertain job releases or for periodic relief at the policy level. Their livelihoods grow dependent on a concentrated system that employs few.

Meeting this challenge calls for institutional design, not passive placement. Can the public share the ownership and returns of the intelligence dividend? Can the barriers to calling on foundational compute and tools come down, so individuals and micro-enterprises hold the capacity to run economic activity on their own? Can subsistence stop binding itself to the condition of being employed by a single firm?

This deepens the U.S.–China contrast: the American debate on technology dividends tries to build a direct income conduit to individuals after corporate payrolls shrink; China prefers to pour factors into the industrial end, expecting a stronger system to carry employment along.

AI's evolution weakens the historical basis for "enlarge first, employment follows." Higher production automation blunts the employment pull. From salt and iron to compute, the core choice runs continuous: when the state's capacity to create wealth leaps upward, how does it — while strengthening industry — grant ordinary people more room for autonomous development, rather than treating them as inputs serving production?

VIII. Epilogue: Balance Inside and Outside the City Gate

If waiting for top-down carry-over remains the only expectation, those left outside the gate of growth will not stay silent forever.

Today's "new marginal population" has not left the cities. They scatter across shared rentals and screens, waiting for the algorithm's next gig assignment. Ancient vagrants lost their land; today's frustrated knowledge workers lose the ascent channel through which skill once accumulated into assets and a settled life. When mobility stalls, marginalization can pass between generations: families without accumulation constrain the next generation's access to education and development resources, and cyclical career pain hardens into durable stratification. The record of dynastic order and collapse teaches one lesson: populations adrift from the system, with livelihoods unsettled, remain the deepest variable of social stability.

Domestic distributive choices are also shaped by the external geopolitical environment.

The Sanders-style dividends and rights legislation opening this essay mark only one face of America's response to technological shock; at Washington's strategic level, the other face looms larger — technology competition elevated to national rivalry and geopolitical advantage. Chip controls, supply-chain restructuring, and compute contests all intensify external pressure.

That external pressure further entrenches the domestic "industry first, manufacturing supreme" path dependence. The more compute, chips, energy, and advanced manufacturing count as strategic resolve, the more factors concentrate on technological assault and capacity building. Under grand considerations of guarding against external risk, the urgency of labor-rights protection and distributive innovation slides down the ordering.

One common calculus in policy trade-offs: at a critical stage of industrial breakthrough, concentrating force on supply-side bottlenecks appears to yield greater economy-wide benefits than an early shift of resources into redistribution; livelihoods can be patched once the industrial base stands firm, at fiscal and efficiency cost that appears more controllable.

Yet historical experience warns that deferring the distributive gap exacts higher long-run institutional costs. For groups displaced by technology with formal ascent channels narrowing, abstract future prosperity cannot substitute for present survival dignity and security.

As established channels for sharing growth keep narrowing, the relative threshold of unconventional paths falls. History proves it again and again: when wealth growth cannot reach the masses, the foundation of prosperity stands unstable; those denied a slice of the pie will not wait outside the city gate forever — for marginalized groups with the proper road blocked, storming Chang'an has always been easier than testing one's way in.

text:
Die amerikanische Besetzung Deutschlands Klaus-Dietmar Henke 1995

Part 1

Imagine living in Germany in the spring of 1945. Your country is collapsing. Cities have been reduced to ruins, families have been scattered, children have been evacuated from their homes, and millions of people face an uncertain future. German soldiers are retreating, American armies are advancing, and the government that demanded loyalty and sacrifice is disintegrating. For ordinary civilians, the question is no longer whether Germany will win the war. It is whether their families, homes, and communities will survive its final weeks.

In Die amerikanische Besetzung Deutschlands, German historian Klaus-Dietmar Henke reconstructs the American conquest and occupation of Germany from the summer of 1944 to the Potsdam Conference in 1945. Drawing on military records, administrative documents, eyewitness accounts, and contemporary German sources, he reveals a period in which Germany’s political order collapsed, civilians endured extraordinary suffering, and foreign military authorities assumed control over the defeated country.

The destruction of German towns and the deaths of civilians

In April 1945, the war continued to devastate German communities even when defeat was unavoidable. Henke documents the destruction inflicted during the American advance through northern Württemberg and Baden, where German military resistance prolonged fighting that could no longer change the outcome of the war.

During the first three weeks of April, at least 200 towns, villages, and hamlets in the area were directly affected by combat. Henke records 2,170 civilian deaths, including 596 in the Heilbronn district alone. Approximately 4,500 buildings—including homes, churches, schools, barns, and stables—were completely destroyed.

In Königshofen an der Tauber, German defenders included teenage naval cadets alongside regular troops and SS formations. By the time American forces occupied the town, approximately 75 percent of its buildings had been destroyed. Thirteen inhabitants were dead. In Ödheim, where Waffen-SS troops continued resisting, ten days of fighting left 35 inhabitants dead and approximately 120 buildings destroyed.

For the civilians who survived, the devastation extended far beyond the immediate deaths. Houses that had sheltered generations of families disappeared. Farms lost their barns and livestock facilities. Churches and schools were destroyed. Families emerged from shelters to discover that the places where they had lived and worked no longer existed.

The refugees prevented from reaching American territory

As Germany collapsed, enormous numbers of civilians fled westward, hoping to escape the approaching Soviet army. For many, reaching American-held territory appeared to offer the possibility of greater security.

Henke describes the desperate circumstances along the Elbe, where refugees crowded the eastern bank seeking passage. German military commanders estimated that approximately 100,000 civilians were waiting in one area, although subsequent estimates suggested the number might have been substantially higher.

American commanders initially imposed restrictions on civilian crossings. This meant that men, women, and children who had already endured the collapse of their communities could find themselves prevented from reaching the opposite bank, even when American soldiers were visible across the river.

Henke records that an unknown number of refugees were overtaken by Soviet troops while attempting to reach the western side. He also recounts the escape of a German family with a sick five-month-old baby, whose father managed to persuade an auxiliary policeman to permit their crossing despite an American prohibition.

The episode demonstrates how military orders governing surrender and movement could determine the fate of civilian families who had no influence over those decisions.

…..Says a lot about why things are the way they are in US  Government!
A DC 'airport ticket agent' offers some examples of why the US is in so much trouble!
1 I had a New Hampshire Congresswoman (Carol Shea-Porter) ask for an aisle seat so that her hair wouldn't get messed up by being near the         window. (On an airplane!)
2   I got a call from a Kansas Congressman's (Moore) staffer (Howard Bauleke), who wanted to go to Cape Town .
I started to explain the length of the flight and the passport information, and then he interrupted me with,
''I'm not trying to make you look stupid, but Cape Town is in Massachusetts .''
Without trying to make him look stupid, I calmly explained, ''Cape Cod is in Massachusetts ,
Cape Town is in South Africa ..''
His response -- click..
3   A senior Vermont Congressman (Bernie Sanders) called, furious about a Florida package we did.
I asked what was wrong with the vacation in Orlando . He said he was expecting an ocean-view room.
I tried to explain that's not possible, since Orlando is in the middle of the state.
He replied, 'Don't lie to me!, I looked on the map, and Florida is a very THIN state!!'' (OMG)
4   I got a call from a lawmaker's wife (Landra Reid) who asked,
''Is it possible to see England from Canada ?''
I said, ''No.'' She said, ''But they look so close on the map'' (OMG, again!)
5   An aide for a cabinet member (Janet Napolitano) once called and asked if he could rent a car in Dallas ..
I pulled up the reservation and noticed he had only a 1-hour layover in Dallas ...
When I asked him why he wanted to rent a car, he said,
''I heard Dallas was a big airport, and we will need a car to drive between gates to save time.'' (Aghhhh)
6   An Illinois Congresswoman (Jan Schakowsky) called last week.
She needed to know how it was possible that her flight from Detroit left at 8:30 a.m.,
and got to Chicago at 8:33 a.m.
I explained that Michigan was an hour ahead of Illinois ,
but she couldn't understand the concept of time zones.
Finally, I told her the plane went fast, and she bought that.
7   A New York lawmaker, (Jerrold Nadler) called and asked,
''Do airlines put your physical description on your bag so they know whose luggage belongs to whom?''
I said, 'No, why do you ask?'
He replied, ''Well, when I checked in with the airline, they put a tag on my luggage that said (FAT),
and I'm overweight. I think that's very rude!''
After putting him on hold for a minute, while I looked into it. (I was dying laughing).
I came back and explained the city code for Fresno , Ca. is (FAT - Fresno Air Terminal),
and the airline was just putting a destination tag on his luggage..
8   A Senator John Kerry aide (Lindsay Ross) called to inquire about a trip package to Hawaii .
After going over all the cost info, she asked,
''Would it be cheaper to fly to California and then take the train to Hawaii ?''
9   I just got off the phone with a freshman Congressman, Bobby Bright from Ala. who asked,
''How do I know which plane to get on?''
I asked him what exactly he meant, to which he replied, ''I was told my flight number is 823,
but none of these planes have numbers on them.''
10   Senator Dianne Feinstein called and said, ''I need to fly to Pepsi-Cola , Florida .
Do I have to get on one of those little computer planes?''
I asked if she meant fly to Pensacola and fly on a commuter plane.
She said, ''Yeah, whatever, smarty!''
11   Mary Landrieu, La. Senator, called and had a question about the documents she needed in order to
fly to China .
After a lengthy discussion about passports, I reminded her that she needed a visa.
"Oh, no I don't.
I've been to China many times and never had to have one of those.''
I double checked and sure enough, her stay required a visa.
When I told her this she said, ''Look, I've been to China four times and every time
they have accepted my American Express!''
12   A New Jersey Congressman (John Adler) called to make reservations,
''I want to go from Chicago to Rhino, New York .''
I was at a loss for words. Finally, I said, ''Are you sure that's the name of the town?''
'Yes, what flights do you have?'' replied the man.
After some searching, I came back with,
''I'm sorry, sir, I've looked up every airport code in the country and can't find a rhino anywhere."
''The man retorted, ''Oh, don't be silly! Everyone knows where it is. Check your map!''
So I scoured a map of the state of New York and finally offered,
''You don't mean Buffalo , do you?''
The reply? ''Whatever! I knew it was a big animal.''
Now you know why the Government is in the shape it's in!

text:
On 9th October, 25 days before the US midterms, President Trump eased Russian diesel sanctions while Ukrainian negotiators were in Miami discussing peace. No reciprocal halt to attacks on Ukraine’s energy system was announced with the deal. 

On 13th September, Trump publicly told Zelensky to stop targeting Russian diesel infrastructure, citing fuel shortages. Kyiv said it would support an energy ceasefire if Russia also stopped its attacks.

Now Treasury’s General License 135 permits Russian diesel transactions, including US imports, through 7th April 2027.

Zelensky told Axios he would support energy sanctions relief tied to a reciprocal halt in attacks on energy facilities.

The Kremlin’s account offered no immediate return to peace talks. Putin would consider when negotiations could resume.

Ukraine’s refinery campaign has helped constrain Russian fuel production. Diesel prices also reflect reduced refining elsewhere, including China and the Middle East, according to EIA. 

The strategic risk for Kyiv is that hurting Russia’s fuel supply also creates pressure in Washington to restrain Ukraine.

Russia has received permission to make diesel sales previously restricted by US sanctions. Cheaper fuel for Americans still depends on deliveries and market conditions. 

Kyiv is still asking what restraint Moscow will offer in return.

text:
Everyone is being promised cheaper diesel from Russia, but President Trump’s 9th October announcement assigns no specific tonnage to the US.

The schedule is over 300,000 tons immediately, another 500,000 in November and 1 million afterward, for American and global markets. The largest tranche, another 3 million tons, explicitly depends on Russia’s refinery condition.

Washington has authorized Russian diesel imports through 7 April 2027. Moscow says it is beginning to lift its export restrictions early.

Both governments can remove trade barriers while damaged refineries still limit production.

Russia does not need every refinery repaired to export some fuel. But permission to sell does not establish how much additional diesel will reach the world market, rather than move between buyers.

POTUS Trump gets a supply announcement 25 days before the midterms. Putin gets access to sales previously restricted by US sanctions.

The price question is how much extra fuel actually arrives, where and when. The announcement alone cannot answer it.

text:
Shubho Mahalaya 🪔
Mahalaya carries two meanings in one quiet dawn.
🌾 Remembering: It is the last day of Pitru Paksha, when families offer water and food to their ancestors, including those whose dates are no longer known. It's gratitude, not grief.
🔱 Welcoming: In East India, it marks the start of Devi Paksha. Maa Durga is invoked to leave Kailash for her earthly home, and artisans traditionally paint the eyes of the idol, Chokkhu Daan, on this day.
The story at its heart is from the Devi Mahatmya, where the gods' combined energies take the form of Durga to defeat the buffalo-demon Mahishasura. The early-morning radio recitation of Mahishasura Mardini, a Bengali tradition for generations, retells it. For many, it just isn't Durga Puja until that voice fills the house at 4 AM.
Seven days to Shashthi. 🥁
Where are you celebrating this year? 👇

text:
That's not all...
National under Key formed confidence and supply deals with the Maori Party from 2008 to 2017. That partnership produced the 2010 endorsement of UNDRIP and helped keep the government stable while the Paris Agreement was ratified in 2016.

The Māori Party used its position to lock in several lasting changes. Coleader Pita Sharples flew to New York without prior public notice and announced New Zealand’s support for UNDRIP, reversing the previous Labour refusal. National the traitors called it purely aspirational, yet the decision later supplied the foundation for the Hepuapua roadmap. UNDRIP has never been mandated and does not apply to New Zealand it never will as Maori are not indigenous to New Zealand.

The party also secured the repeal of the Foreshore and Seabed Act and its replacement by the Marine and Coastal Area Act 2011, the launch of Whanau Ora, a guarantee that Maori seats would not be removed without Maori consent, and roughly $3 billion in targeted budget gains. Symbolic steps such as flying the Tino Rangatiratanga flag on the Auckland Harbour Bridge further shifted the political tone toward partnership language.

In the 2017 negotiations Bill English’s National team offered fewer cabinet roles and fewer policy concessions than Labour. Reports at the time put National’s offer at around three positions, not all inside cabinet, while New Zealand First sought four cabinet seats plus one outside. 

Labour’s package included four cabinet posts, an under-secretary, the Deputy Prime Ministership and Foreign Affairs for Winston Peters. National’s party organisation also resisted major policy ground on immigration, foreign investment and regional development. Peters therefore chose Labour.

That choice kept New Zealand First inside government as a handbrake through 2020. The party blocked a full capital gains tax, restrained some Green Party priorities and moderated immigration settings. Labour did the dirty on New Zealand First after promising not to move forward on Hepuapua in that time. 

Once voters left New Zealand First below the threshold in 2020, Labour gained an absolute majority and moved quickly on co-governance measures, the Māori Health Authority, expanded Treaty clauses and the wider He Puapua agenda that had been prepared under the earlier UNDRIP commitment.

The post-2020 period therefore reflected both the earlier Māori Party gains under National and the absence of the New Zealand First restraint that had limited Labour from 2017 to 2020.

text:
7.7 magnitude earthquake rocks Panama: Historical churches collapse, "major disaster" declared (photos) 

A powerful earthquake with a magnitude of 7.7 was recorded yesterday (09) in the southern region of Panama, a Central American state. The earthquake, which occurred at 12:56 PM local time in Panama (11:26 PM Sri Lanka time), had its epicenter approximately 12 km west-southwest of a rural area called Pitaloza Arriba in Herrera province, at a shallow depth of 12.6 km below the Earth's surface.
This location is situated approximately 200 km southwest of the capital, Panama City, and the world-renowned Panama Canal.

The United States Geological Survey (USGS) initially reported the earthquake's magnitude as close to 8.0 but later revised it to 7.7. According to their estimates, approximately 4.6 million people felt the tremor, with nearly 43,000 living in areas that experienced severe shaking.

Panama's Institute of Geosciences states that this earthquake is linked to the Azuero-Soná fault system. Such powerful earthquakes are rare in Panama, which is located in a complex zone where the Cocos, Nazca, and Caribbean tectonic plates converge.

The University of Panama reports that more than 45 aftershocks were recorded after the main earthquake. The strongest of these was a magnitude 6.6 tremor that occurred approximately two and a half hours later. The USGS has warned of a high probability of further tremors exceeding magnitude 5 in the coming week.

The most significant damage occurred in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera, Los Santos, and Coclé. In the city of Penonomé, located midway between the epicenter and the capital, a part of the cathedral tower collapsed, and the governor's office also sustained damage. In the same city, the rear section of the "Dos Continentes" hotel collapsed onto parked vehicles.

In Playa Venao, a popular tourist town in Los Santos province, a section of a multi-story building collapsed, crushing several vehicles. Local reports suggested people might be trapped inside, but this has not yet been confirmed. The colonial-era San Atanasio church in Los Santos, designated a national historical heritage site since 1938, also collapsed.

Roads around the epicenter have cracked and completely collapsed, and it is reported that access to the Tonosí area of Los Santos by land has been lost. Houses in areas including Las Minas in Herrera province have cracked, and power supply was disrupted in six provinces. The operation of several water treatment plants was also affected.

"We are scared. It's just the two of us, elderly, living here. The house is cracked, and we are afraid it will collapse on us," said 74-year-old Ricardo Brown, a resident of Las Minas, to the media.

Strong tremors were also felt in Panama City, 200 km away, and people were evacuated en masse from tall buildings. Services on two metro lines were temporarily suspended, and debris fell in some areas. However, no serious structural damage to the capital's skyscrapers has been reported.

After emergency safety procedures and inspections, the Canal Authority announced that operations at the Panama Canal were proceeding as normal. The Cobre Panamá copper mine is also reported to be operating normally. Flights at Tocumen International Airport were briefly halted for safety checks but later resumed. Schools nationwide were closed, and coincidentally, a national earthquake evacuation drill was scheduled for next Monday.

According to the latest reports, no fatalities have been confirmed from this earthquake. Omar Smith, head of Panama's Civil Protection Agency (Sinaproc), and Deputy Head Malitzi Rivera stated that there are a few minor injuries, including one person injured by falling debris in Penonomé. Assessing the situation in difficult-to-reach areas is still challenging due to road damage and communication disruptions.

President José Raúl Mulino declared the situation a "major disaster" and urged the public to remain calm, stating that "what happened should not be used to create fear or chaos." He visited Penonomé and toured a hospital where patients were being treated outdoors. Several countries have offered assistance.

The USGS estimates that Panama's economic loss could be between 1% and 10% of its GDP, and attention has also been drawn to the risks of soil liquefaction and landslides.

Following the earthquake, tsunami warnings were issued for coastal areas in countries including Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Guatemala, El Salvador, and Mexico. However, the United States Tsunami Warning System later confirmed that the threat had passed. It noted that minor sea-level fluctuations might still occur around the epicenter.

This is considered another powerful earthquake in the region, following deadly earthquakes earlier this year in Venezuela and Colombia.

text:
THE UNPAID HOUR
It is three in the morning inside a sterile short-time hotel room. The air conditioner is rattling faintly in the background. A sixty-year-old man is lying flat on his back, staring at the ceiling. Next to him is a thirty-year-old woman. They aren’t sleeping, and they aren't touching.

He is talking. He’s talking about his estranged daughter, his brutal divorce, and how terrified he was to fly to Thailand because he thought the entire experience would make him feel dirty. She is just listening. She isn’t scrolling through her phone. She is looking directly at him.

The bar fine was already settled. The short-time rate is sitting securely in her purse. The transaction technically ended twenty minutes ago, and she has absolutely no financial obligation to stay awake for this. But she is listening anyway. She is exhausted, her feet hurt from the heels, but she listens because he is talking about the terrifying prospect of dying alone—something that quietly echoes in her own head. She doesn't offer empty platitudes or fake a giggly smile. She simply rests her hand heavily on his shoulder. The room goes quiet. A minute later, his breathing slows, and he falls asleep. She lies there, staring at the same ceiling, not thinking about the money she just made. She is thinking about her own father, whom she hasn't seen in five years.

There is a strange, quiet phenomenon on the neon grid that completely shatters the cynical logic of the veteran expat: genuine emotional intimacy often takes root directly inside relationships that were exclusively designed to be financial transactions. It isn't a rare exception. It is a recurring pattern.

The money doesn't magically disappear, but it fades into the background, making room for a connection that cannot be reduced to just sex or cash. This happens through three very specific mechanics. The first is time. A standard transaction is an hour. But when a customer returns three, four, five times, that hour stretches. He talks. She listens. It stops being a service and becomes a bridge. The second is vulnerability. The man is shielded by the fact that he is paying. He can confess his deepest fears, his shame, the things he could never tell his ex-wife, precisely because he knows this woman on the payroll won't judge him. He opens up, and in return, she stops seeing a walking ATM and starts seeing a human being. The third is recognition. She remembers how he holds his glass, what he refuses to talk about, and the fact that he was actually kind to her when he didn't have to be.

Western observers usually want to force this dynamic into two comfortable boxes: either he is a naive idiot buying fake love, or she is a ruthless predator faking a smile. Both versions are incredibly lazy.

He isn't stupid. He knows exactly how the grid works, and he knows she is on the clock. But he feels something anyway, not because he is being scammed, but because he is profoundly lonely. Intimacy isn't a commodity you can purchase, but it also isn't a commodity that money prevents from forming. And she isn't a predator. She is simply a woman doing a job, and doing a job doesn't magically erase your humanity. She gets tired, she feels pity, and sometimes, despite all her rigid defenses, she actually gets attached. The paradox is that the transaction doesn't prevent the intimacy; it frames it. The money creates a safe boundary, and inside that boundary, something real occasionally breathes.

But this grey zone is incredibly dangerous for both of them.

For her, catching feelings makes an already brutal job almost impossible to survive. If she actually cares, she can't just switch her emotions off when the next customer buys her a drink. She knows that if she reveals her true attachment, he might use it against her, or worse, pack his bags and leave her completely broken. So she stays silent. She smiles, she goes to work, and she buries whatever real emotion she felt.
For him, the danger is believing that the frame has vanished entirely. The connection feels so intensely real that leaving the country becomes a psychological agony. He flies home to an empty house, constantly texting her, clinging to the memory of someone actually listening to him. He thinks it is true love. She won't correct him. The feeling is real enough for him to survive another year in his cold reality.

Morning breaks over Pattaya. He is still sleeping heavily. She quietly gathers her things, being careful not to wake him. She grabs a hotel pen and writes a quick note on a napkin. Not "thank you." Not "goodbye." Just See you.

She steps out onto Soi Buakhao. The street is dead, littered with empty bottles and exhausted motorcycle taxi drivers waiting by the curb. She climbs onto a bike, heading back to her cramped room, her mind already shifting back to the relentless rhythm of survival—she needs to sleep, she needs to eat, she needs to buy rice.

Back at the bar where she works, a cardboard coaster with a faded "PU" logo sits wet with condensation from the night before. No one has wiped the table yet. It will sit there until evening, and then it will be thrown away. Just like everything else on the grid.

But the man sleeping in the hotel won't forget. He won't necessarily remember her exact name or the shape of her face in a few years, but he will remember the profound, anchoring sensation that for one unpaid hour in the middle of the night, someone actually sat beside him and listened. It wasn't a fairy tale romance. It was human proximity. It happened, it ended, and for a while, it was enough.

When I posted earlier today that Subsidy is gone forever, some doubted including some progressive friends who did so silently.

But if there is one thing I can boast of, it's my ability to cut through the noise and analyse what is before me.

And it's shocking that a lot of people really failed to understand what yesterday's press conference by the Minister of Finance Taiwo Oyedele was all about.

To be clear, the MAJOR takeaway was PRICE MODULATION!

Discount by NNPCL Retail is a side note and that is purely a commercial decision by NNPCL, which before now offered a N66 per litre discount on their own to celebrate Nigeria's 66th independence just like any commercial venture would do.

I'm glad that the Finance Minister this night explained in layman's language that this NNPCL discount is NOT subsidy.

Reduction in price by a single petrol seller DOES NOT amount to subsidy.

Subsidy is when you sell below your cost price with someone paying the balance.

In the case of NNPCL Retail, they are selling at the cost price. Mind you NNPCL Retail get their stock from Dangote Refinery and Dangote is selling to them at market price with his own profit margin on top. So, NNPCL is simply foregoing their PROFIT! How on earth is this subsidy?

I will take my time and write an Explainer on the major element that Nigerians should be talking about - PRICE MODULATION - and why it's very important for us considering how quickly prices of consumer goods rice in Nigeria whenever fuel prices go up due to crude oil prices going up and how slowly these same commodity prices come down even when crude oil prices begin to fall sharply.

I will also later come at the ignorant Atiku, Obi and their supporters who for one reason or the other seem not to understand this simple distinction and are urinating all over social media that subsidy is back.

text:
Pitru Paksha: A Fortnight of Remembrance and Gratitude

Pitru Paksha, also known as Shraddha Paksha, is a sacred 16-day period in our Sanatana lunar calendar dedicated to honouring one’s ancestors. It falls during the Krishna Paksha of Bhadrapada or Ashwin and concludes today on Sarva Pitru Amavasya, also called Mahalaya Amavasya. On this day, offerings are traditionally believed to reach all ancestors, those whose death tithis are known, those long forgotten, and those whose names have faded from living memory.

In the framework of Sanatana Dharma, every individual is born with three primary debts: to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors. Pitru Rina, the debt owed to one’s forefathers, is considered foundational because the present generation exists only because of those who came before. The rites performed during Pitru Paksha-especially Tarpan, Pind Daan, and Shraddha-are viewed as the principal means of discharging this debt. According to texts such as the Garuda Purana and Brahma Purana, the souls of the departed draw closer during this period. Offerings of water mixed with black sesame seeds, rice balls, and food are believed to provide them sustenance and peace in the subtle realm.

The practice is not merely ritualistic. It is an expression of gratitude and continuity. Ancestors are remembered not only as biological predecessors but as the carriers of values, culture, and the very possibility of life. When these rites are performed with sincerity, tradition holds that the ancestors become pleased and, in turn, bless the family with health, harmony, prosperity, and the removal of obstacles. Conversely, prolonged neglect is sometimes associated with what is called Pitru Dosha-recurring difficulties in the family that are believed to stem from unfulfilled ancestral obligations.

Beyond the spiritual dimension, Pitru Paksha serves a quiet social purpose. It gathers dispersed families around a shared duty. It preserves lineage memory in an age when birth and death dates are easily lost in the noise of modern calendars. It also encourages charity-feeding the needy, poors, cows, and even crows, which are symbolically linked to the ancestors in several regional traditions.

Today, as Pitru Paksha draws to a close, the emphasis shifts from individual tithi-based remembrance to a collective offering for the entire lineage. For many households, Sarva Pitru Amavasya is the most practical and encompassing day of the year. One does not need elaborate arrangements; sincerity of intention, a simple offering of water and food, and a moment of quiet recollection are considered sufficient.

In a time when individual achievement is often celebrated above everything else, Pitru Paksha offers a gentle corrective. It reminds us that no one stands alone. The lives we lead rest on the unseen labour, sacrifices, and affections of those who are no longer present. Honouring them is not an act of superstition; it is an act of civilisational memory and personal humility.

As the fortnight ends and the festive season of Navratri begins tomorrow, may we carry forward not only the rituals but the underlying spirit-gratitude for the past, responsibility toward the present, and care for the continuity of the family line.

I met a woman through an online community about two years ago.

We initially bonded over our shared interest in movies, but our conversations eventually became much more personal.

We talked almost every day.

We discussed our families, relationships, jobs, and the things we were struggling with privately.

Although we'd never met in person, I considered her one of my closest friends.

She told me she lived in California, worked in marketing, and was saving money to start her own business.

Whenever she had a difficult day, I'd encourage her.

When I got promoted at work, she was one of the first people I told.

Everything seemed normal until she mentioned that she was having trouble paying her rent.

She didn't directly ask me for money, but she described her situation in a way that made me feel I should offer to help.

I eventually sent her $300 because I genuinely believed she was in a difficult position.

She promised to repay me when things improved.

A few weeks later, she disappeared from our usual conversations.

I wasn't particularly concerned until another member of our online community contacted me privately.

She asked whether I'd ever met my friend in person.

When I said no, she told me that several people had discovered inconsistencies in the woman's stories.

Apparently, she had used different names in different online communities.

I decided to investigate.

8 Things You Need to Know about Surveillance
8 important truths about surveillance
ai-in-society
Author
Rachel Thomas

Published
August 7, 2019

Over 225 police departments have partnered with Amazon to have access to Amazon’s video footage obtained as part of the “smart” doorbell product Ring, and in many cases these partnerships are heavily subsidized with taxpayer money. Police departments are allowing Amazon to stream 911 call information directly in real-time, and Amazon requires police departments to read pre-approved scripts when talking about the program. If a homeowner doesn’t want to share data from their video camera doorbell with police, an officer for the Fresno County Sheriff’s Office said they can just go directly to Amazon to obtain it. This creation of an extensive surveillance network, the murky private-public partnership surrounding it, and a lack of any sort of regulations or oversight is frightening. And this is just one of many examples related to surveillance technology that have recently come to light.

I frequently talk with people who are not that concerned about surveillance, or who feel that the positives outweigh the risks. Here, I want to share some important truths about surveillance:

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
Data often contains errors
Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
Surveillance changes our behavior
Surveillance disproportionately impacts the marginalized
Data privacy is a public good
We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
While I was writing this post, a number of investigative articles came out with disturbing new developments related to surveillance. I decided that rather than attempt to include everything in one post (which would make it too long and too dense), I would go ahead and share the above facts about surveillance, as they are just a relevant as ever.

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
There is a long history of data about sensitive attributes being misused, including the use of the 1940 USA Census to intern Japanese Americans, a system of identity cards introduced by the Belgian colonial government that were later used during the 1994 Rwandan genocide (in which nearly a million people were murdered), and the role of IBM in helping Nazi Germany use punchcard computers to identify and track the mass killing of millions of Jewish people. More recently, the mass internment of over one million people who are part of an ethnic minority in Western China was facilitated through the use of a surveillance network of cameras, biometric data (including images of people’s faces, audio of their voices, and blood samples), and phone monitoring.

Adolf Hitler meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. in 1937. Source: Computer History
Pictured above is Adolf Hitler (far left) meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. (2nd from left), shortly before Hitler awarded Watson a special “Service to the Reich” medal in 1937 (for a timeline of the Holocaust, see here). Watson returned the medal in 1940, although IBM continued to do business with the Nazis. IBM technology helped the Nazis conduct detailed censuses in countries they occupied, to thoroughly identify anyone of Jewish descent. Nazi concentration camps used IBM’s punchcard machines to tabulate prisoners, recording whether they were Jewish, gay, or Gypsies, and whether they died of “natural causes,” execution, suicide, or via “special treatment” in gas chambers. It is not the case that IBM sold the machines and then was done with it. Rather, IBM and its subsidiaries provided regular training and maintenance on-site at the concentration camps: printing off cards, configuring machines, and repairing them as they broke frequently.

Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
In the above examples, the data collection began before genocide was committed. IBM began selling to Nazi Germany well before the Holocaust (although continued for far too long), including helping with Germany’s 1933 census conducted by Adolf Hitler, which was effective at identifying far more Jewish people than had previously been recognized in Germany.

It is important to recognize how data and images gathered through surveillance can be weaponized later. Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote that “One [hard truth] is that data and surveillance networks created for one purpose can and will be used for others. You must assume that any personal data that Facebook or Android keeps are data that governments around the world will try to get or that thieves will try to steal.”

Plenty of data collection is not involved with such extreme abuse as genocide; however, in a time of global resurgence of white supremacist, ethno-nationalist, and authoritarian movements, it would be deeply irresponsible to not consider how data & surveillance can and will be weaponized against already vulnerable groups.

Data often has errors (and no mechanism for correcting them)
A database of suspected gang members maintained by California law enforcement officials was found to be full of errors, including 42 babies who had been added to the database when they were less than 1 year old (28 of whom were marked as “admitting to being gang members”). Even worse, there was no process in place for correcting mistakes or removing people once they’ve been added.

An NPR reporter recounts his experience of trying to rent an apartment and discovering that TransUnion, one of the 3 major credit bureaus, incorrectly reported him as having two felony firearms convictions. TransUnion only removed the mistakes after a dozen phone calls and notification that the story would be reported on. This is not an unusual story: the FTC’s large-scale study of credit reports in 2012 found 26% of consumers had at least one mistake in their files and 5% had errors that could be devastating. An even more opaque, unregulated “4th bureau” exists: a collection of companies buying and selling personal information about people on the margins of the banking system (such as immigrants, students, and people with low incomes), with no standards on what types of data are included, no way to opt out, and no system for identifying or correcting mistakes.

Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
What makes the examples in the previous section disturbing is not just that errors occurred, but that there was no way to identify or correct them, and no accountability for those profiting off the error-laden data. Often, even the existence of the systems being used is not publicly known (much less details of how these systems work), unless discovered by journalists or revealed by whistleblowers. The Detroit Police Dept used facial recognition technology for nearly two years without public input and in violation of a requirement that a policy be approved by the city’s Board of Police Commissioners, until a study from Georgetown Law’s Center for Privacy & Technology drew attention to the issue. Palantir, the defense startup founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, ran a program with New Orleans Police Department for 6 years which city council members did not even know about, much less have any oversight.

After two studies found that Amazon’s facial recognition software produced inaccurate and racially biased results, Amazon countered that the researchers should have changed the default parameters. However, it turned out that Amazon was not instructing police departments that use its software to do this either. Surveillance programs are operating with few regulations, no oversight, no accountability around accuracy or mistakes, and in many cases, no public knowledge of what is going on.

Surveillance changes our behavior
Hundreds of thousands of people in Hong Kong are protesting an unpopular new bill which would allow extradition to China. Typically, Hong Kong locals use their rechargeable smart cards to ride the subway. However, during the protests, long lines of people waited to use cash to buy paper tickets (usually something that only tourists do) concerned that they would be tracked for having attended the protests. Would fewer people protest if this was not an option?

In the United States, in 2015 the Baltimore Police Department used facial recognition technology to surveil people protesting the death of Freddie Grey, a young Black man who was killed in police custody, and arrested protesters with outstanding warrants. Mass surveillance could have a chilling impact on our rights to move about freely, to express ourselves, and to protest. “We act differently when we know we are ‘on the record.’ Mass privacy is the freedom to act without being watched and thus in a sense, to be who we really are,” Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote in the New York Times.

Flyer from the company Geofeedia Source
Surveillance disproportionately impacts those who are already marginalized
Surveillance is applied unevenly, causing the greatest harm to people who are already marginalized, including immigrants, people of color, and people living in poverty. These groups are more heavily policed and surveilled. The Perpetual Line-Up from the Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology studied the unregulated use of facial recognition by police, with half of all Americans appearing in law enforcement databases, and the risks of errors, racial bias, misuses, and threats to civil liberties. The researchers pointed out that African Americans are more likely to appear in these databases (many of which are drawn from mug shots) since they are disproportionately likely to be stopped, interrogated, or arrested. For another example, consider the contrast between how easily people over 65 can apply for Medicare benefits by filling out an online form, with the invasive personal questions asked of a low-income mother on Medicaid about her lovers, hygiene, parental shortcomings, and personal habits.

In an article titled Trading privacy for survival is another tax on the poor, Ciara Byrne wrote, “Current public benefits programs ask applicants extremely detailed and personal questions and sometimes mandate home visits, drug tests, fingerprinting, and collection of biometric information… Employers of low-income workers listen to phone calls, conduct drug tests, monitor closed-circuit television, and require psychometric tests as conditions of employment. Prisoners in some states have to consent to be voiceprinted in order to make phone calls.”

Data privacy is a public good, like air quality or safe drinking water
Data is more revealing in aggregate. It can be nearly impossible to know what your individual data could reveal when combined with the data of others or with data from other sources, or when machine learning inference is performed on it. For instance, as Zeynep Tufekci wrote in the New York Times, individual Strava users could not have predicted how in aggregate their data could be used to identify the locations of US military bases. “Data privacy is not like a consumer good, where you click ‘I accept’ and all is well. Data privacy is more like air quality or safe drinking water, a public good that cannot be effectively regulated by trusting in the wisdom of millions of individual choices. A more collective response is needed.”

Unfortunately, this also means that you can’t fully safeguard your privacy on your own. You may choose not to purchase Amazon’s ring doorbell, yet you can still show up in the video footage collected by others. You might strengthen your online privacy practices, yet conclusions will still be inferred about you based on the behavior of others. As Professor Tufekci wrote, we need a collective response.

We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
Many people are uncomfortable with surveillance, but feel like they have no say in the matter. While the threats surveillance poses are large, it is not too late to act. We are seeing success: in response to community organizing and an audit, Los Angeles Police Department scrapped a controversial program to predict who is most likely to commit violent crimes. Citizens, researchers, and activists in Detroit have been effective at drawing attention to the Detroit Police Department’s unregulated use of facial recognition and a bill calling for a 5-year moratorium has been introduced to the state legislature. Local governments in San Francisco, Oakland, and Somerville have banned the use of facial recognition by police.

For further resources, please check out: - Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology - Digital Defense Playbook

8 Things You Need to Know about Surveillance
8 important truths about surveillance
ai-in-society
Author
Rachel Thomas

Published
August 7, 2019

Over 225 police departments have partnered with Amazon to have access to Amazon’s video footage obtained as part of the “smart” doorbell product Ring, and in many cases these partnerships are heavily subsidized with taxpayer money. Police departments are allowing Amazon to stream 911 call information directly in real-time, and Amazon requires police departments to read pre-approved scripts when talking about the program. If a homeowner doesn’t want to share data from their video camera doorbell with police, an officer for the Fresno County Sheriff’s Office said they can just go directly to Amazon to obtain it. This creation of an extensive surveillance network, the murky private-public partnership surrounding it, and a lack of any sort of regulations or oversight is frightening. And this is just one of many examples related to surveillance technology that have recently come to light.

I frequently talk with people who are not that concerned about surveillance, or who feel that the positives outweigh the risks. Here, I want to share some important truths about surveillance:

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
Data often contains errors
Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
Surveillance changes our behavior
Surveillance disproportionately impacts the marginalized
Data privacy is a public good
We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
While I was writing this post, a number of investigative articles came out with disturbing new developments related to surveillance. I decided that rather than attempt to include everything in one post (which would make it too long and too dense), I would go ahead and share the above facts about surveillance, as they are just a relevant as ever.

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
There is a long history of data about sensitive attributes being misused, including the use of the 1940 USA Census to intern Japanese Americans, a system of identity cards introduced by the Belgian colonial government that were later used during the 1994 Rwandan genocide (in which nearly a million people were murdered), and the role of IBM in helping Nazi Germany use punchcard computers to identify and track the mass killing of millions of Jewish people. More recently, the mass internment of over one million people who are part of an ethnic minority in Western China was facilitated through the use of a surveillance network of cameras, biometric data (including images of people’s faces, audio of their voices, and blood samples), and phone monitoring.

Adolf Hitler meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. in 1937. Source: Computer History
Pictured above is Adolf Hitler (far left) meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. (2nd from left), shortly before Hitler awarded Watson a special “Service to the Reich” medal in 1937 (for a timeline of the Holocaust, see here). Watson returned the medal in 1940, although IBM continued to do business with the Nazis. IBM technology helped the Nazis conduct detailed censuses in countries they occupied, to thoroughly identify anyone of Jewish descent. Nazi concentration camps used IBM’s punchcard machines to tabulate prisoners, recording whether they were Jewish, gay, or Gypsies, and whether they died of “natural causes,” execution, suicide, or via “special treatment” in gas chambers. It is not the case that IBM sold the machines and then was done with it. Rather, IBM and its subsidiaries provided regular training and maintenance on-site at the concentration camps: printing off cards, configuring machines, and repairing them as they broke frequently.

Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
In the above examples, the data collection began before genocide was committed. IBM began selling to Nazi Germany well before the Holocaust (although continued for far too long), including helping with Germany’s 1933 census conducted by Adolf Hitler, which was effective at identifying far more Jewish people than had previously been recognized in Germany.

It is important to recognize how data and images gathered through surveillance can be weaponized later. Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote that “One [hard truth] is that data and surveillance networks created for one purpose can and will be used for others. You must assume that any personal data that Facebook or Android keeps are data that governments around the world will try to get or that thieves will try to steal.”

Plenty of data collection is not involved with such extreme abuse as genocide; however, in a time of global resurgence of white supremacist, ethno-nationalist, and authoritarian movements, it would be deeply irresponsible to not consider how data & surveillance can and will be weaponized against already vulnerable groups.

Data often has errors (and no mechanism for correcting them)
A database of suspected gang members maintained by California law enforcement officials was found to be full of errors, including 42 babies who had been added to the database when they were less than 1 year old (28 of whom were marked as “admitting to being gang members”). Even worse, there was no process in place for correcting mistakes or removing people once they’ve been added.

An NPR reporter recounts his experience of trying to rent an apartment and discovering that TransUnion, one of the 3 major credit bureaus, incorrectly reported him as having two felony firearms convictions. TransUnion only removed the mistakes after a dozen phone calls and notification that the story would be reported on. This is not an unusual story: the FTC’s large-scale study of credit reports in 2012 found 26% of consumers had at least one mistake in their files and 5% had errors that could be devastating. An even more opaque, unregulated “4th bureau” exists: a collection of companies buying and selling personal information about people on the margins of the banking system (such as immigrants, students, and people with low incomes), with no standards on what types of data are included, no way to opt out, and no system for identifying or correcting mistakes.

Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
What makes the examples in the previous section disturbing is not just that errors occurred, but that there was no way to identify or correct them, and no accountability for those profiting off the error-laden data. Often, even the existence of the systems being used is not publicly known (much less details of how these systems work), unless discovered by journalists or revealed by whistleblowers. The Detroit Police Dept used facial recognition technology for nearly two years without public input and in violation of a requirement that a policy be approved by the city’s Board of Police Commissioners, until a study from Georgetown Law’s Center for Privacy & Technology drew attention to the issue. Palantir, the defense startup founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, ran a program with New Orleans Police Department for 6 years which city council members did not even know about, much less have any oversight.

After two studies found that Amazon’s facial recognition software produced inaccurate and racially biased results, Amazon countered that the researchers should have changed the default parameters. However, it turned out that Amazon was not instructing police departments that use its software to do this either. Surveillance programs are operating with few regulations, no oversight, no accountability around accuracy or mistakes, and in many cases, no public knowledge of what is going on.

Surveillance changes our behavior
Hundreds of thousands of people in Hong Kong are protesting an unpopular new bill which would allow extradition to China. Typically, Hong Kong locals use their rechargeable smart cards to ride the subway. However, during the protests, long lines of people waited to use cash to buy paper tickets (usually something that only tourists do) concerned that they would be tracked for having attended the protests. Would fewer people protest if this was not an option?

In the United States, in 2015 the Baltimore Police Department used facial recognition technology to surveil people protesting the death of Freddie Grey, a young Black man who was killed in police custody, and arrested protesters with outstanding warrants. Mass surveillance could have a chilling impact on our rights to move about freely, to express ourselves, and to protest. “We act differently when we know we are ‘on the record.’ Mass privacy is the freedom to act without being watched and thus in a sense, to be who we really are,” Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote in the New York Times.

Flyer from the company Geofeedia Source
Surveillance disproportionately impacts those who are already marginalized
Surveillance is applied unevenly, causing the greatest harm to people who are already marginalized, including immigrants, people of color, and people living in poverty. These groups are more heavily policed and surveilled. The Perpetual Line-Up from the Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology studied the unregulated use of facial recognition by police, with half of all Americans appearing in law enforcement databases, and the risks of errors, racial bias, misuses, and threats to civil liberties. The researchers pointed out that African Americans are more likely to appear in these databases (many of which are drawn from mug shots) since they are disproportionately likely to be stopped, interrogated, or arrested. For another example, consider the contrast between how easily people over 65 can apply for Medicare benefits by filling out an online form, with the invasive personal questions asked of a low-income mother on Medicaid about her lovers, hygiene, parental shortcomings, and personal habits.

In an article titled Trading privacy for survival is another tax on the poor, Ciara Byrne wrote, “Current public benefits programs ask applicants extremely detailed and personal questions and sometimes mandate home visits, drug tests, fingerprinting, and collection of biometric information… Employers of low-income workers listen to phone calls, conduct drug tests, monitor closed-circuit television, and require psychometric tests as conditions of employment. Prisoners in some states have to consent to be voiceprinted in order to make phone calls.”

Data privacy is a public good, like air quality or safe drinking water
Data is more revealing in aggregate. It can be nearly impossible to know what your individual data could reveal when combined with the data of others or with data from other sources, or when machine learning inference is performed on it. For instance, as Zeynep Tufekci wrote in the New York Times, individual Strava users could not have predicted how in aggregate their data could be used to identify the locations of US military bases. “Data privacy is not like a consumer good, where you click ‘I accept’ and all is well. Data privacy is more like air quality or safe drinking water, a public good that cannot be effectively regulated by trusting in the wisdom of millions of individual choices. A more collective response is needed.”

Unfortunately, this also means that you can’t fully safeguard your privacy on your own. You may choose not to purchase Amazon’s ring doorbell, yet you can still show up in the video footage collected by others. You might strengthen your online privacy practices, yet conclusions will still be inferred about you based on the behavior of others. As Professor Tufekci wrote, we need a collective response.

We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
Many people are uncomfortable with surveillance, but feel like they have no say in the matter. While the threats surveillance poses are large, it is not too late to act. We are seeing success: in response to community organizing and an audit, Los Angeles Police Department scrapped a controversial program to predict who is most likely to commit violent crimes. Citizens, researchers, and activists in Detroit have been effective at drawing attention to the Detroit Police Department’s unregulated use of facial recognition and a bill calling for a 5-year moratorium has been introduced to the state legislature. Local governments in San Francisco, Oakland, and Somerville have banned the use of facial recognition by police.

For further resources, please check out: - Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology - Digital Defense Playbook
