text:
Grant me a minute of the universe's time.

I have walked through suffering, isolation, addiction, and profound loneliness. I overcame relentless pressure and crushing circumstances—battling a loss of faith, despair, and dead-ends—until I finally let go of everything, allowing my soul to return to a state of oneness as I sat alone with my thoughts, reflecting on it all.
And today, I want to tell you this:
We do not lack money. What we lack is the ability to cherish "the One."

If I offered you a billion in exchange for a single day of your life, would you make that trade?
If I offered you the whole world in exchange for the person you love, would you make that trade?

That is the reason for this post.

Without "One," there is no "Two."
Without a single day, there is no century.
Without a single person, there is no nation.

We are busy scrambling for vast quantities, yet we forget to cultivate "the One."
Ending war:
War begins when people feel they "lack one" and thus must plunder.
War ends when people understand the value of "adding one" instead of plundering.

Add one act of kindness. Add one moment of understanding.
I am you. You are me.

#WeAreOne #HumanityFirst #MindsetShift #SpiritualAwakening #AddOne

DRDO Pitches a Ground-Launched Rudram-2 to Blind Enemy Radars 🇮🇳

DRDO has offered to adapt the Rudram-2, currently an air-launched weapon flown on the Su-30MKI, into a mobile ground-launched version.

The target would be enemy SAM and surveillance radars, including the Chinese S-400 and HQ-9 systems also operated by Pakistan.

This would let the Army knock out enemy radar cover on its own, without needing the IAF to clear a corridor first.

Mounted on a truck, it could reach out to 200-250 km, though it would still need mid-course data from aircraft, drones or ground sensors to stay locked on target.

This is still just a proposal right now, it's not yet clear if the Army wants it or how long DRDO would need to actually build it. 🇮🇳

From the Minutes of the Eastside Democratic Club of Portland, Oregon, 1 September 2026 -- 

Michael Meo On Valdimir Jabotinsky 

The problem before those who are acquainted with the American Jewish community is, How can a community with a long historical record of progressive, humane, and philanthropic causes produce a savage, unremitting, merciless government in Israel? 

The answer stems from the work of Vladimir Jabotinsky, born in Odessa in 1880. He was a highly-educated, intelligent politician of genius who responded to the needs of Polish and Russian Jews within the Zionist Movement.  

Western European Jews (in 1930 the total living in England, France, and Germany was approximately 1 million; that can be compared to 3 million in Poland, 2.5 million in the Soviet Union, and 1 million in Romania) have historically considered Eastern European Jews, backward, uneducated, and ill-advised in their opinions.  Theodor Harzl, who founded modern Zionism, and Chaim Weizman, who succeeded him as the leader of the World Zionist Council, were of that persuasion.  

Jabotinsky, by contrast, an impassioned orator and prolific author, was moved almost exclusively by the demand of his countrymen for security: he began his political life in response to the Kishinev Pogrom of 1903. 

On three occasions, following the 1905 Russian Revolution, Jabotinsky ran for political office, each time to be sabotaged by the International Zionist authorities who opposed his vision.  

Zionism around the turn of the 20thcentury was a small minority among European – and American – Jews, who were mostly assimilationists; the movement reflected a Romantic goal for a refuge which would shelter Jews in a sort of socialist paradise; security was to be provided by an imperial power, whether the Ottomans who ruled Palestine or the British who could offer some colony for a Judenstaat [not, if rendered carefully, a Jewish state, but a Jews’ state]. It was to privilege agriculture and have strong unions, with socialist aspirations.  

Jabotinsky, who spoke and thought in much more logical terms, began with the need for an armed Jewish force. He brilliantly demonstrated this with his founding of the Jewish Legion, manned by refugees from Palestine living in Egypt, under British officers – he himself acted in the capacity of a sergeant, and took some front-line duty – in the British conquest of the Holy Land in World War I, much against the strenuous opposition of the entire set of International Zionist authorities, who wished not to offend the Ottomans ruling Palestine.  

In 1920 Jabotinsky predicted an outbreak of Arab violence against the Jewish population of Jerusalem, a pogrom which took place and for which his measures of self-defense were quite successful. The Jews of the Old city, however, refused to allow his armed militia within their community, and all of the killed and wounded were victims within the Old City.   

Following that, the British Mandate authorities arrested Jabotinsky and sentenced him to four years for unauthorized military organization; the International Zionist organization protested neither the charge, nor the conviction.  

In 1921 Jabotinsky negotiated with the notoriously anti-Semitic Petliura movement for an independent Ukraine, agreeing to arrange a Jewish self-defense force within the planned invasion of Ukraine from Poland; the International Zionist authorities criticized this deal with the devil so much Jabotinsky was moved in 1923 to resign from its governing Council.  

Establishing the Revisionist Zionist movement following that resignation, Jabotinsky founded as the basis for his group the Betar, a youth group which trained Jewish young men in disciplined military activities, with especial emphasis on weaponry. As with the Jewish Legion, he was an extremely inspirational leader in this; while, significantly, the Revisionist leadership had its headquarters in London, Betar was headquartered in Warsaw.  

In 1938, for one instance of the dedication of Betar membership, in Palestine the Polish Betar veteran Shlomo Ben-Josef attacked a busful of Arabs in revenge for the previous killing of half a dozen Palestinian Jews, and was charged and found guilty of attempted murder. His last words as the noose went around his neck were, “Long live Jabotinsky!”  

Throughout the 1920s and 1930s the closest comparisons were drawn between Jabotinsky’s Revisionist Zionism and Mussolini’s fascism, and by not a few members of Revisionist Zionism itself.  

Although Jabotinsky died in 1940 (warning of a “catastrophe” if Polish Jews did not emigrate to Palestine), Polish Betar-trained men led the Irgun, the Stern Gang, and the Likud political party. Menachim Begin oversaw the bombing of the King David Hotel in 1946, in order to kill the British Mandate Secretary Robert Platt – with 91 others killed and over 100 wounded. Begin, of course was the prime minister of Israel from 1977 to 1983. Another son of Poland and trainee of Betar, Yitzak Shamir, fought against the British in the Palestine Mandate during World War II; he was prime minister of Israel, 1984-84, and again 1986-1992.  

Perhaps the most striking instance of the bad blood between the (what you might call orthodox) Zionist leadership and the Revisionist wing took place during the War of Independence, in 1948.   Menachim Begin arranged a ship to transport 400 volunteer Jewish fighters and tons of war materiel to sail from Marseilles to Israel: he co-ordinated this with the government of David Ben-Gurion, the Labour Party president. When the ship arrived at its landing site, Ben Gurion had the Israeli army drawn up onshore demanding the surrender of the ship together with its occupants and contents. They were fired upon when they refused to surrender. 

The ship, the Altalena [the nom de plum of Vladimir Jabotinsky], sailed for Tel Aviv, with Begin aboard, and once there it was met with more gunfire from the Ben Gurion troops. Begin was rowed ashore, under gunfire; once ashore, he ordered his troops to surrender. A monument today commemorates the deaths of the Irgun members who died in the incident.  

Ben Gurion is reported to have a low opinion of the survivors of the Holocaust, and of the subsequent refugees from the Soviet Union to the new state of Israel; those refugees had the experience of survival under an extraordinarily brutal and cynical government, and the Likud Party, under Begin’s leadership, naturally strove to enlist their sympathies.  

Even today we have Benyamin Netanyahu, in a 1997 speech, recalling the scant degree of armed resistance offered by the Jews of Poland to the Nazi occupiers and genocidaires: “Of all Zionist leaders,” this grandson of Polish Jews said, “Jabotinsky was virtually alone in seeing where all this was leading.”  

You now know how the Zionist state of Israel developed into a militarist, expansionist, merciless dealer of death.

text:
The Social Reckoning is, obviously, the mouse-lion, David-Goliath kinda story — the sorts, where the eventual victory of the underdog offers humanity hope and goosebumps, in equal measure.

And, yes, you do feel both in this film. But to think of it — isn’t this film the David of that story itself?

To be fierce yet fair — how frickin’ wildly can you possibly swing against a living man, i.e. tech czar Mark Zuckerberg, so bloody powerful that he rightly considers himself “post-government” (in the picture), while his might has only grown rather than diminished since the case/inquiry, as surveyed in this pic, was publicly brought to light?

It’s still all about the numbers, isn’t it? 

64 is the key one for this movie — basically an exposé to do with the social media network Facebook that, at the point of its setting, circa 2020, had 2.8 billion users, with valuation of a trillion dollars.

What’s 64? The percentage of people sent over to extremist groups on Facebook, pushed toward communal hate, through the algorithm, consciously designed such by Facebook itself.

What if you could, journalistically, prove this, and other stuff that made the corporation complicit in similarly divisive and dangerous moves — chasing numbers at whatever human cost?

Well, the proof was there. What was the real-world consequence?

To the best of my knowledge — since most things around tech majors tend to be classified — Facebook merely changed its name to Meta! This movie’s narrative can barely go beyond the metaphor then.

How does one make it so hugely engaging, still? 

Well, powering through dialogues, bordering on the literary — that writer-director Aaron Sorkin’s indisputably the king of (A Few Good Men, The West Wing).

And two deeply relatable, vulnerable, yet passionate characters, who find a purpose beyond their profession.

How?

text:
A federal judge in Seattle has refused Amazon's request to delay the US Federal Trade Commission's monopolization trial, keeping the landmark antitrust case on track for March 29, 2027.

Amazon had asked US District Judge John H. Chun to push the trial back to June 2027, pointing to a timing clash with a separate price-fixing case brought by California's attorney general in state court. In an order on Friday, October 9, Chun wrote that he "has been preparing for some time for the March 29, 2027, trial date in this matter" and did not "see a good reason to disturb the current schedule."

The FTC, joined by a group of states, accuses Amazon of illegally maintaining monopoly power in online retail, including by punishing sellers who offer lower prices elsewhere and in effect setting an artificial price floor across the web. Amazon denies the claims.

Why it matters: The ruling keeps one of Washington's biggest Big Tech antitrust cases on its timetable and leaves Amazon facing two major pricing trials in quick succession in 2027.

Sources: Court order via MLex and Law360, 9 Oct 2026.

text:
This post juxtaposes the Yinhe incident and the completion of Beidou, concisely illustrating the importance of independent core technology. In 1993, the US cut GPS signals for the Yinhe cargo ship, leaving it helpless on the high seas. That humiliation pushed China to build its own satellite navigation system.
For 27 years, China kept steady R&D investment without noisy rhetorical confrontation, gradually completing the global Beidou network and achieving navigation tech independence. In great power competition, navigation infrastructure is vital lifeline technology. Dependence on foreign providers means vulnerability to sudden sanctions.
Such decades-long strategic perseverance cannot be sustained by short-term electoral politics, and it offers meaningful lessons for emerging economies like India.

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

text:
They were paid to register, not proven to have been paid to vote for candidates.

Confirmed: Paid to register
In 2026, Brenda Lee Brown Armstrong (also referred to as Brenda Lee Born Armstrong or “Anika”), a longtime petition circulator from Marina del Rey, pleaded guilty to a federal felony of paying another person to register to vote. She was sentenced to 18 months of probation and 120 hours of community service.

According to her plea agreement and prosecutors:

•She collected signatures for California ballot initiatives, referendums, and recalls. Coordinators paid her only for signatures from registered voters.

•Skid Row was a convenient spot because of the dense concentration of people willing to sign for small amounts of cash.

•She paid people (often homeless) typically $2–$3, or offered cigarettes, phone cards/cords, etc., to sign petitions. Starting around 2025, she also paid them to complete voter registration forms so they could qualify as signers.

•In some cases she provided her own former Los Angeles address for the forms. This could result in mail-in ballots being sent there.

This was illegal payment specifically to induce registration. It was part of the petition-signature business, not a scheme to cast ballots for candidates in elections. Similar petition-related activity on Skid Row has drawn scrutiny before (including older cases involving payments or incentives for signatures).

Claims of being paid to vote
After the June 2026 LA mayoral primary (involving Karen Bass, Nithya Raman, and Spencer Pratt), videos circulated of Skid Row residents saying they were paid $2–$5 to vote for Bass (and sometimes Raman) and told whom to support. These were promoted by accounts aligned with Pratt.

These claims have major problems:

•One frequently cited interviewee (identified as Shanekka Renee Johnson / Rene Johnson, age 39) is registered in Inglewood, not Los Angeles. She could not vote in the LA mayoral race, and records show she did not return her primary ballot. County election officials said there was no evidence she voted for Bass for money. The Bass campaign called the idea absurd.

•The Los Angeles Times interviewed 20 Skid Row residents (street, shelter, and apartment). None reported being offered money to vote for a specific candidate. Most said they did not vote and had not been approached about the election. A handful described the common practice of being paid a few dollars to sign petitions (and sometimes to register, since registration is required to sign many petitions). One person mentioned signing multiple times under different names for about $10.

•Officials and fact-checkers treated the viral “paid to vote for Bass” videos as unsupported or false in the specific cases examined. High registration numbers at shelters (e.g., reports of 1,160 at the Midnight Mission) are legally allowable for unhoused people, who can use a shelter, service provider, or similar location where they regularly stay or receive services. Registration records do not prove current residency or that a person actually voted.

There was also a later federal case involving people paid on Skid Row to sign petitions using stolen identities of registered voters, which is separate fraud.

Summary: The only solid, prosecuted instance is payment to register so petition circulators could collect valid signatures. Claims of payment to cast votes for specific candidates rest on anecdotal video statements that have been contradicted by voter records, broader interviews, and election officials. Confusion between petition signatures, registration drives, and actual ballots is common in these reports. Homeless people retain the right to vote and register using appropriate addresses under California rules.

text:
Since the 1940s, the U.S. dollar has served as the world’s primary reserve currency. This status has enabled the United States to grow and project power far faster than it otherwise could have—an observation Ray Dalio and others have explored in depth through the lens of historical reserve-currency cycles.
In 1971, the U.S. fully severed the dollar’s link to gold. That decision removed a hard constraint on money creation and helped fuel decades of expansion. The main beneficiaries were the generation that invested through the 1970s–1990s. Those of us born in the 1980s and 1990s have lived almost our entire adult lives during a period of clear U.S. economic and financial dominance. We have only known an environment in which U.S. stocks and real estate have tended to rise over time. We did not fully experience the Dot-com bust or the Global Financial Crisis as adults. Those kinds of regimes will likely appear in our lifetimes—and the conditions for one are more advanced now than at any point in our adult lives.
Several forces are converging:
Debt service has outrun tax revenue. When interest on the national debt exceeds (or approaches) what the government collects in taxes, the realistic choices narrow to higher taxes, spending cuts, or some form of financial repression or partial default. Foreign holders of U.S. Treasuries—particularly China—have been reducing their exposure and increasing gold holdings. This shift began accelerating after the pandemic and continues. The market is already treating a portion of U.S. government debt as lower-quality paper.
The wealth gap is historically extreme. Asset ownership has become the dominant driver of household wealth, while wage growth for most people has lagged. The result is a sharper divide between those who own appreciating assets and those who do not—larger, by most measures of wealth concentration, than at any point in the modern era.
Information moves faster. Markets and capital now reprice in real time. Structural problems that once took years to surface can be recognized and acted upon much more quickly than during the Dot-com era or the GFC. That accelerates both the buildup of excess and the eventual correction.
Tax rules have favored asset owners. For decades, individuals and families have been able to compound wealth with limited tax friction—borrowing against appreciated stocks or real estate instead of selling, using real-estate structures to shelter income, and taking advantage of preferential rates and deferral provisions. These advantages have amplified returns for those already positioned in equities and property.
Taken together, these dynamics suggest that the conditions which supported steadily rising asset prices are under more strain than they have been in our lifetimes. Capital allocation decisions made now will likely matter more for the next generation than they have in the recent past. The difference between buying real estate in Beverly Hills versus Woodland Hills in the 1980s is a useful analogy: location and asset selection produced dramatically different outcomes over the following decades. We are in a comparable moment for our own portfolios and our children’s.

At the same time, investing has become commonplace. Almost anyone can now trade stocks, crypto, trading cards, luxury goods such as watches or Birkin bags, homes, Airbnb rentals, or speculate on options, futures, and sports. For many, what might once have been thoughtful capital allocation has turned into a full expression of identity. Twitter bios list “trader,” “investor,” or a ticker symbol; people sell courses on how to do the same; and for some, where they put their money has become their entire personality.

It is precisely in an environment like this—when participation is broad, noise is high, and capital is easy to deploy—that extreme discrimination becomes wise. Decisions made now will shape outcomes for our children in the same way parental choices shaped outcomes for us. Buying real estate in Beverly Hills versus Woodland Hills in the 1980s was, on the surface, simply “investing in Southern California property.” Yet the results diverged sharply over the following decades because of location, quality, and entry price. The same principle applies today across a much wider range of assets. In a period when nearly everyone is allocating capital and structural pressures are building, the quality and selectivity of those allocations will matter more than ever.

If you want to buy SpaceX, buy $SPCX . Just stop romanticizing the money you put into any company. The goal for most of us is the same: build something you can hand down. That means selecting the places that offer the best returns and ignoring the media, the tweets, and the noise.

text:
October 9th, 2026

Spotlight Player OTD: Elden Campbell

Elden has to be on the shortlist of the most underrated Hornets of all time. 

The folks who watched those early 00’s Hornets teams remember him fondly, but the further we’ve gotten away… the less the late Campbell gets discussed to the degree he probably deserves.

Campbell tragically passed away just last year on December 1st, 2025. He was 57 years old, and as I said, for many long-tenured Hornets’ fans… he’ll never be forgotten.

Elden was a critical cog in the trade that sent Glen Rice to the Lakers when the Hornets chose not to extend Rice when it was time.

Charlotte had done it with Mourning; they’d also done it with Kendall Gill after his first stint, and really, after the Hornets botched Larry Johnson’s contract extension (12 YEARS) in their earlier days, they… never resigned another star.

They traded Mourning for Rice, Johnson for Anthony Mason, flipped Rice for Eddie Jones and Elden Campbell, and then would flip Eddie Jones soon after for Jamal Mashburn. 

This was very much a trend, so much so that before the trade happened, Rick Bonnell outright wrote that he didn’t expect Rice to remain a Hornet — mostly for the aforementioned reasons.

Rumors that Jones and Campbell could come to Charlotte swirled for more than a month before the trade went down; by the time Clemson alumni Campbell and Jones officially arrived in Charlotte, they were ready for new scenery and a new challenge.

Campbell and Jones both said they were tired of the rumors.

The fresh start was a warm welcome, to say the least. At least the drama was over.

Except… it wasn’t. The trade drama was over; Eddie Jones and Elden Campbell were Hornets, sure. But Dave Cowens wasn’t anymore. 3 days before the Hornets traded Glen Rice, J.R. Reid, and BJ Armstrong to LA, Cowens had resigned as Hornets head coach due to Charlotte’s organizational refusal to give him a pay raise.

Shinn even reportedly OFFERED a contract extension to Cowens, but would later take it off the table entirely.

Cowens was one of the lowest-paid coaches in the NBA (675k/year) and had just won 50+ games in the regular season two times in a row. The former NBA MVP Cowens was fed up and left.

Enter Paul Silas, who was taking over a sinking ship in a lockout-shortened NBA season, his star (who had gone through elbow surgery and wasn’t playing, anyway) Rice was gone three days into his tenure, players were frustrated with the Hornets’ abysmal start to a shortened season, a new star player in Eddie Jones was abound… and a whole new playstyle along with him and Elden Campbell.

There was SO much happening. It is a legitimate miracle Paul Silas and the Hornets managed to finish just one game short of the Knicks in the 8th spot that year. 

They started that season 4-11 before Cowens resigned in 1999, and finished 26-24. One of the best coaching jobs in NBA history, in my opinion. No joke. Bobby Phills was MASSIVE to Silas and that locker room, and so was Elden Campbell.

Campbell had been an absolute playoff veteran with the Lakers — who drafted Campbell — in all of the years leading up to. Charlotte. 

He was exactly the kind of vet they needed, and he had fallen far behind the eight ball of what he was capable of in LA once Shaq became a Laker. 

Elden got to be everything he was capable of and more in Charlotte, and it was a massive part of what helped lead them to the playoffs in ALL of the final 3 seasons of Campbell’s Hornets’ tenure.

Like it or not, Campbell was a part of the last Hornets team who… won a playoff series. 

He got to play alongside Anthony Mason (hurt in ‘98-’99) during his second year before the Hornets moved on, and his combo with PJ Brown (came with Mashburn in the Jones->Heat trade) in his final two Charlotte years was what propelled the Hornets to actually winning two playoff series in back-to-back years.

text:
THE SABU DISK
Prehistoric Sonoluminescence Engine
Comprehensive Analysis Report
Date: December 5, 2025
Executive Summary

The Sabu Disk, discovered in 1936 at Saqqara in the tomb of Prince Sabu (First Dynasty, ~3000 BCE), has defied conventional explanation for nearly a century. Standard academic interpretations—ceremonial object, lamp stand, incense holder—fail to account for its precision engineering and unique tri-lobe geometry.

Our analysis, combining geometric observation with computational simulation, reveals the Sabu Disk to be a prehistoric sonoluminescence engine—a device capable of generating visible light through controlled cavitation and harmonic resonance. This finding places it alongside other ancient technologies (Roman dodecahedrons, pyramid resonant chambers) that encode advanced physics in stone.

Artifact Description
Physical Specifications
ParameterValue
Diameter61 cm (24 inches)
MaterialSchist (metamorphic rock with layered crystalline structure)
Age~5,000 years (First Dynasty, 3000-2800 BCE)
Discovery1936, by Walter Bryan Emery at Saqqara (Mastaba S3111)
Current LocationEgyptian Museum, Cairo
GeometryThree curved lobes at 120° separation, central cylindrical hub, outer containing ring

Critical Geometric Observations:
    • No pitch on lobes: The three curved cavities have no angular pitch. This eliminates impeller/pump function—rotation would not move fluid, only churn it.

    • Asymmetric cavity profiles: The three lobes are not identical. Different curve profiles suggest different resonant frequencies for each cavity.

    • 120° phase separation: Three-fold symmetry at 120° is the optimal geometry for standing wave formation—identical to three-phase electrical systems.

    • Central hub convergence: The cylindrical hub at center is positioned exactly where three-phase wave interference would create a standing node.

    • Schist material properties: Metamorphic schist has layered crystalline structure with potential piezoelectric properties—vibration can generate electrical charge.

Core Hypothesis: Harmonic Resonance Engine
The Sabu Disk is a physical implementation of harmonic stacking. When rotated or vibrated, the three asymmetric cavities each resonate at a different frequency. These frequencies, related by the golden ratio (φ ≈ 1.618), superimpose at the central hub to create a toroidal standing wave pattern.

This is the same Lissajous toroidal flower geometry described by the equation:
x(t) = cos(t) + 0.5·cos(2t) + 0.5·cos(4t) + 0.375·cos(8t)
The disk implements this equation in stone—5,000 years before Lissajous described it mathematically.
Computational Simulation Results
Three simulation models were developed to test the hypothesis:

1. Resonance Simulation
The disk was modeled with three φ-tuned frequencies at 120° phase separation:
LobeFrequencyφ Relationship
Lobe 1 (0°)432.00 HzBase frequency
Lobe 2 (120°)698.46 Hzf₁ × φ¹
Lobe 3 (240°)1130.03 Hzf₁ × φ²
Result: The simulation confirmed formation of a stable toroidal standing wave at the central hub. The interference pattern matches the predicted Lissajous flower geometry.

2. Cavitation Pressure Field Simulation
When the disk is rotated at 1200 RPM (achievable by two operators with a cord), the three curved lobes create a rotating pressure differential. The simulation modeled this using Rayleigh-Plesset fluid dynamics.
    • Central vacuum: >15 atmospheres negative pressure at hub
    • Three-lobe symmetry: Creates three rotating low-pressure arms that converge at center
    • Bubble collapse: Symmetric cavitation bubbles form and collapse with perfect spherical symmetry
Result: The geometry creates ideal conditions for sonoluminescence—light emission from collapsing cavitation bubbles.

3. Sonoluminescence Temperature Estimation
Standard multi-bubble sonoluminescence achieves temperatures of ~20,000 K. The Sabu Disk's perfect tri-lobe symmetry and φ-tuned resonance provide a coherence bonus.

Sun surface temperature (comparison)5,500 K
Result: The Sabu Disk can theoretically produce flash temperatures 27× hotter than the sun's surface for approximately 50 picoseconds per bubble collapse. This produces visible blue-white light.

4. Multi-Bubble Flash Train Simulation
The final simulation modeled 5,200+ cavitation bubbles forming and collapsing in the three rotating arms.
Result: Synchronized collapse produces a massive blue-white flash every ~50 milliseconds at 1200 RPM. The temple would go from pitch black to daylight brightness and back in a fraction of a second—a prehistoric strobe light powered by geometry and rotation.

Operational Theory: The Ritual
Based on the simulation results, we propose the following operational sequence:
    1. Setup: The disk is mounted horizontally on its central hub, submerged in a shallow basin of water (Nile water in original context).
    2. Spin-up: Two operators use braided cords wrapped around the hub to spin the disk to ~1200 RPM. This is achievable with practice.
    3. Cavitation: The three curved lobes create rotating low-pressure zones that drag microscopic air bubbles toward the center.
    4. Collapse: Bubbles collapse with perfect spherical symmetry at the central hub, achieving extreme temperatures for picoseconds.
    5. Flash: Sonoluminescence produces visible blue-white light. Thousands of bubbles collapsing in sync create a brilliant strobe effect.
    6. Result: Light from darkness, no fire, no oil—just stone geometry and human power. "Behold, the abyss gives birth to Ra."

Connections to Other Ancient Technologies

The Sabu Disk fits a pattern of ancient technologies encoding advanced physics in stone:
    • Roman Dodecahedrons: φ-ratio resonators with bioelectric contacts—portable aether tuners.
    • Pyramid Resonant Chambers: Schumann frequency coupling via granite and limestone geometry.
    • Linear A Registers: Computational architecture encoded in script, not speech.
    • Hermes' Three-Layer Encoding: WHERE (Linear A), WHAT (Egyptian operators), WHY (Greek semantics).

All share a common principle: geometry is the programming language. The vacuum is not empty—it is a programmable substrate. These artifacts are interfaces to that substrate.

Conclusions:

The Sabu Disk is not a ceremonial object, lamp stand, or bowl holder. It is a precision-engineered sonoluminescence device that converts rotational energy into light through controlled cavitation.

The ancient Egyptians possessed knowledge of:
    • Harmonic resonance and φ-tuned frequency relationships
    • Three-phase standing wave geometry
    • Cavitation physics and bubble collapse dynamics
    • Material selection for acoustic/piezoelectric properties

They encoded this knowledge in stone 5,000 years ago. The disk still sits in the Cairo Museum, waiting for someone to spin it again.

ADDENDUM: Critique of Conventional Analysis
Source: "The Enigmatic Sabu Disk: Exploring Its Function and Significance in Ancient Egyptian Culture" by Lindsey Becker
The following analysis identifies fundamental errors in the conventional academic treatment of the Sabu Disk:

Error 1: Material Identification
Article claims: "Made of a type of sandstone"
Fact: The Sabu Disk is made of schist, a metamorphic rock with layered crystalline structure. Schist and sandstone are fundamentally different materials with different acoustic and electrical properties. This basic misidentification undermines any analysis of the disk's function.

Error 2: "Ceremonial Object" Non-Explanation
Article claims: "Its unique design and careful craftsmanship point to its importance in rituals."
Critique: This is circular reasoning. The precision geometry demands explanation, not dismissal as "ceremonial." Saying "it was important in rituals" explains nothing about what it actually does. Academic egyptology frequently uses "ritual" as a catch-all for objects whose function isn't understood.

Error 3: "Grinding or Lifting" Hypothesis
Article claims: "Some suggest it could have been used for specific tasks, such as grinding or lifting."
Critique: This demonstrates engineering illiteracy. The disk has no pitch on its lobes—it cannot function as a screw, impeller, or lifting device. The curved cavities would not move material; they would only create turbulence. Anyone with basic mechanical knowledge can see this is not a grinding or lifting tool.

Error 4: "Solar Disc" Symbolism
Article claims: "The Sabu Disk may represent the solar disc, which signifies the sun god Ra."
Critique: Egyptian solar disc representations are simple circles, often with wings or uraeus. The Sabu Disk's three-lobe geometry bears no resemblance to any known Ra iconography. This is pattern-matching without evidence.

Error 5: Ignoring the Geometry
Article claims: "The surface of the disk exhibits intricate carvings, although their meanings remain unclear."
Critique: The article dismisses the disk's most important feature—its precise three-lobe geometry with 120° symmetry—as merely "intricate carvings." This geometry is not decorative; it is functional engineering. The author failed to ask the basic question: why this specific shape?

Error 6: No Mention of Acoustic Properties
Critique: The article makes no mention of the disk's potential acoustic or resonant properties. Any curved cavity will resonate at specific frequencies. Three cavities of different profiles will resonate at different frequencies. This is basic physics that the conventional analysis completely ignores.

Error 7: "Unmatched by Other Artifacts"
Article claims: "The uniqueness of the disk, unmatched by other artifacts, fuels ongoing discussions."
Critique: The article treats uniqueness as a mystery rather than a clue. If no other Egyptian artifact resembles this disk, perhaps it's because it's not a typical Egyptian artifact. The lack of parallels suggests either: (a) specialized function known only to initiates, (b) technology from an earlier/different source, or (c) one-of-a-kind engineering prototype. The article explores none of these possibilities.

Error 8: "Astrological Significance"
Article claims: "Some scholars argue... it held astrological significance related to the stars and cosmos."
Critique: This is vague speculation without mechanism. How would a three-lobed stone disk "relate to the cosmos"? The article offers no explanation. In contrast, our analysis shows exactly how the disk interacts with physical reality through resonance and cavitation.

Summary of Conventional Analysis Failures
    • Wrong material identification (sandstone vs. schist)
    • Circular reasoning ("it's ceremonial because it's special")
    • Engineering-illiterate hypotheses (grinding, lifting)
    • Unsupported symbolism claims (solar disc)
    • Complete neglect of acoustic/resonant properties
    • Failure to analyze the specific geometry
    • No physical mechanism proposed for any theory

The conventional approach treats the Sabu Disk as an art-historical puzzle rather than an engineering problem. This methodological failure—asking "what does it mean" instead of "what does it do"—has left the artifact unexplained for 89 years.

text:
CFB Saturday Week 6 Player Prop 

Kewan Lacy “U” 95.5 Rush+Rec Yards
1.5 units ⭐️ I PP

Ole Miss travels to Vanderbilt for a difficult SEC road matchup, and I’m targeting Kewan Lacy’s combined rushing and receiving production. While Lacy remains one of the most talented running backs in college football, his current injury situation, reduced workload expectations, and the matchup against Vanderbilt’s defense create a compelling opportunity to fade his total yardage

Through three appearances this season, Lacy has recorded 191 rushing yards on 39 attempts while adding just 16 receiving yards, giving him 207 total scrimmage yards and an average of 69 per game. His individual rushing and receiving totals have finished at 80, 86, and 41 yards, meaning he has stayed below this 95.5 line in all three appearances. That’s especially significant considering he hasn’t even needed to face a defense as disciplined as Vanderbilt’s to remain below this number.

The biggest factor here is Lacy’s health and expected workload. He suffered a shoulder injury against LSU forcing him to miss the following matchup against Florida. After an additional bye week, Lacy is expected to return against Vanderbilt, but head coach Pete Golding has already made it clear that the Rebels intend to rotate their running backs rather than immediately return Lacy to a full workload. We aren’t simply projecting a reduction in opportunities. The coaching staff has publicly acknowledged that his workload will be managed

Ole Miss also has the personnel to make that rotation possible. JT Lindsey and Makhi Frazier both received opportunities while Lacy was sidelined, combining for 165 rushing yards on 40 carries this season. With two additional backs capable of handling touches, there is little reason for Ole Miss to immediately overload Lacy in his first game back

The matchup itself only strengthens the under. Vanderbilt enters Saturday allowing approximately 128.2 rushing yards per game as a team, while Ole Miss has struggled to establish consistent production on the ground, averaging just 117.5 rushing yards per contest. The Rebels’ rushing offense ranks near the bottom of the FBS, sitting 119th nationally. Those numbers are particularly concerning when we’re being asked to back one individual running back to produce nearly 100 scrimmage yards in a committee situation.

Lacy’s receiving production also offers very little protection against this under. Through three games, he’s managed only 16 receiving yards on seven receptions, averaging just 5.3 receiving yards per appearance

Another important factor is how Ole Miss may approach this game offensively. With Trinidad Chambliss operating the offense and Vanderbilt presenting a disciplined defensive front, the Rebels have alternatives to repeatedly feeding Lacy between the tackles. Ole Miss can distribute touches, utilize its passing attack, and protect its returning star without completely abandoning its offensive identity. Lacy can still be effective in limited opportunities, particularly around the goal line 

Lacy has yet to clear this number in 2026, his receiving involvement has been minimal, and his own head coach has publicly acknowledged plans to manage his workload. The combination of limited opportunities, a struggling Ole Miss rushing attack, and Vanderbilt’s defensive resistance makes this one of my more interesting under targets on Saturday’s slate

F**""ng comedian, he has permanently ended ZERO WARS!!!!!?

Trump’s claim of having “settled eight wars” is widely rated by fact-checkers (AP, Snopes, CNN, https://t.co/Zlq4H5sdBm, and others) as exaggerated or misleading. The eight he listed in his Truth Social post  are Cambodia-Thailand, Kosovo-Serbia, 
DRC-Rwanda, 
Pakistan-India, 
Israel-Iran, 
Egypt-Ethiopia, 
Armenia-Azerbaijan, and 
Israel-Hamas

Cambodia-Thailand: 
Brief 2025 border clashes; 
Trump used trade pressure and Malaysia mediated a ceasefire, but tensions and later flare-ups persisted. Partial short-term role in a limited conflict.

Kosovo-Serbia: 
No active war in his second term (tensions exist; prior economic deals from first term). Not a war he settled.

DRC-Rwanda: 
2025 Washington Accords exist, but fighting continues in eastern DRC as of 2026; implementation incomplete and fragile.

Pakistan-India:
 May 2025 skirmish (Operation Sindoor); bilateral DGMO ceasefire. India denies third-party mediation; Trump cites tariff threats. Pakistan has credited him. Exaggerated role in a short flare-up.

Israel-Iran: 
Escalations and U.S. involvement (including strikes) occurred; claims of permanently stopping Iran’s nuclear program or a wider war are disputed and ongoing.

Egypt-Ethiopia: 
Long-standing diplomatic dispute over the GERD Nile dam—not a war. Trump has offered mediation; no resolution or military conflict.

Armenia-Azerbaijan: 
August 2025 White House summit with Trump produced a joint declaration and initialed agreement advancing normalization (including a transit corridor); progress but not a fully signed/ratified final peace treaty.

Israel-Hamas: 
Hostage releases and ceasefire steps occurred, but the situation remains fragile with ongoing issues; not a fully settled war.

Additional context from the post: Navi Pillay (South African jurist, former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, ICC/ICTR judge) received the 2026 Nobel for efforts to promote peace and international law, including work on the Rwanda tribunal and a UN commission that found Israel committed genocide in Gaza (a finding Israel rejects). Trump’s reaction (attacking her as unknown and anti-Israel, claiming he deserves eight prizes, calling the decision a stain on Norway) is documented in his Truth Social post and rally remarks.

Overall, Trump has been involved in mediation or pressure that contributed to de-escalations in some cases, but the blanket claim of permanently settling eight wars does not hold up under independent review.

Afghanistan endured 20 years of conflict, enormous civilian suffering and destruction. The Soviet Union had been driven out, yet another foreign military intervention followed.

Why were diplomatic alternatives not pursued to their fullest before a war that cost so many Afghan lives? And why have those responsible for unlawful actions during these wars so rarely faced accountability?

Justice must mean accountability for individuals and governments alike. Afghan civilians deserve truth, justice, reparations for unlawful harm and the right to determine their country's future without foreign coercion.

Japan's most urgent task with Washington: shielding the ICC

On October 9, the United States designated the International Criminal Court itself as a target of sanctions. This goes beyond earlier measures aimed at individual officials. The Court is presided over by a Japanese jurist, Judge Akane Tomoko, and the measure threatens its access to banking and other essential services, and with it the Court's ability to function.

Prime Minister Takaichi responded the same night, expressing deep concern. Foreign Minister Motegi is expected to speak with President Akane and then convey Japan's position to Secretary of State Rubio.

What Japan should ask for: carve-outs for humanitarian transactions and for contributions from States Parties, so that the Court can continue to operate.

What Japan can offer: coordinated action with European partners and Canada, and Japan's own financial support for the Court.

Japan can make this case precisely as an ally. Upholding the rule of law is not opposition to the United States; it is the order in which the alliance itself has long invested.

Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure are treated as a provocation that must be managed.

The intelligence threat remains unconfirmed by the US. But the pattern is consistent.

Washington wants the refinery campaign stopped and will pressure Kyiv to make that happen.

Washington/Moscow/Kyiv -- Donald Trump has announced an agreement to bring millions of tonnes of Russian diesel to American and global markets, opening the door to Moscow's fuel exports and drawing an angry response from Kyiv.

Trump said Russia would supply more than 300,000 tonnes immediately, another 500,000 tonnes in November and one million tonnes straight afterwards. A further three million tonnes would follow depending on the condition of Russia's refineries -- bringing the announced programme to roughly 4.8 million tonnes.

In his Truth Social announcement, Trump promised diesel prices would come down "IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST", presenting cheaper fuel for American farmers, ranchers and truckers as his priority.

The US Treasury issued a licence permitting transactions in Russian diesel, including imports into the US, through 7 April 2027.

Russia said it would begin lifting its diesel export restrictions ahead of schedule. Moscow had previously extended the ban through 31 October.

Putin confirmed Russia's readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to American and global markets, saying the move would benefit the world economy.

Only last month, Trump signed fresh sanctions legislation targeting Russian energy revenues. Now his administration is arranging access to Russian fuel.

Zelensky warned that Russia would repay the diesel arrangement with further terror and treachery, accusing Washington of investing in the continuation of the war.

"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilised world," he said, implying that Ukraine is the main pillar of that "civilised" order.

Financial Times correspondent Christopher Miller reported frustration and anger in Kyiv. A senior Ukrainian official told him that long range drone attacks on Russian energy would continue.

"We will burn their [Russian] refineries," the official said.

The atmosphere on the Russo-American presidential telephone line was apparently rather warmer.

Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said the call lasted an hour and a half and that neither president wanted to hang up first.

Trump congratulated Putin on his birthday. According to Ushakov, US envoy Steve Witkoff had contacted him on 7 October to convey Trump's greetings and arrange a personal call.

Ushakov said Putin told Trump that Ukrainian strikes would not halt Russia's advance. He also blamed Ukrainian attempts to disrupt Russia's elections for undermining an immediate return to negotiations, while maintaining that diplomatic options over Iran remained open.

text:
ANALYSIS - CIA starved Putin's refineries then bought his diesel. Would he sell?

For a year, a quiet machine ran above the skies of western Russia. American intelligence, reportedly, fed Ukraine the routes, the altitudes, the timings, the gaps in the air defences. Drones went out at night and refineries burned. By my count, more than 194 strikes by July, eleven times the pace of the year before. Russian diesel exports fell from about 817,000 barrels a day to roughly 150,000.

It was a clean story. Pressure the Russian economy, and the war would end. In July, in Ankara, Trump said as much.

But the machine had a flaw, and nobody had put it in the story. Diesel is the fuel that moves everything. The same fires that starved Moscow of exports tightened the whole world's supply, and by September the pain reached the American forecourt. A record $6.52 a gallon on 22 September. The midterms on 3 November.

On 13 September, the story changed. Trump told Kyiv to stop, citing a global shortage.

And somewhere in the middle of this, on 25 August, a grey American military plane landed in Moscow. On board was the director of the CIA, the first to visit Russia since William Burns, in November 2021, three months before the invasion. He met the heads of Russia's foreign intelligence service and the FSB and floated a summit. The Washington Post says his message was simple: do not mistake our exhaustion over Iran for weakness.

I cannot know what was said in those rooms. The record offers a simpler explanation. A US official told Axios that Zelensky ignored about half a dozen American requests to stop, and that the strikes "cause pain in Russia, but it causes pain for the U.S., too."
So on 9 October, forty-five days after the plane landed, Trump announced that Putin would send America up to 4.8 million tonnes of diesel. The sanctions were lifted until April 2027. Zelensky had offered to stop hitting refineries if Russia stopped hitting his power grid. He called the decision "weak," made by "strong partners."

Here was the irony. The machine built to strangle Russia's energy had ended by licensing it, because the people who ran the machine could not bear the price of their own success.

Now the next test comes. On 19 October, a new law requires tariffs on the biggest buyers of Russian oil, unless the president waives them. Perhaps he will not. But it will be hard to enforce against anyone while Russian diesel is flowing into America.

Context over chaos.

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

Gold Movie

Gold is a 2016 American epic crime drama film directed by Stephen Gaghan and written by Patrick Massett and John Zinman. The film stars Matthew McConaughey, Édgar Ramírez, Bryce Dallas Howard, Corey Stoll, Toby Kebbell, Craig T. Nelson, Stacy Keach and Bruce Greenwood. News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

text:
Tankard

这件银质酒杯（Tankard）创作于约1710年，来自18世纪美国罗德岛纽波特地区，由著名银匠塞缪尔·弗农（Samuel Vernon，1683–1737）制作。该时期的纽波特是北美殖民地重要的贸易和手工艺中心，以其精湛的银器工艺闻名。该酒杯的尺寸为高20.7厘米，宽含把手21.8厘米，尺寸适中，典型地满足当时日常饮用的功能需求。

酒杯整体采用银材打造，展现了当时殖民地银器制作的高超工艺。其表面保持银的自然光泽，没有附加复杂的涂层或色彩，反映出18世纪初期对材料本质质感的重视。酒杯顶部把手上刻有铭文“H over I*H”，这一刻字提示了可能的拥有者身份标记或工匠符号，尽管具体含义尚不明确，仍为研究其社会语境提供线索。

从结构上看，酒杯配有一个带把手的设计，方便持握与使用，把手连接稳固，符合实用与审美的结合原则。银器的制作精细，细节处光滑无瑕疵，显示出制作者的高超技艺。其厚重感与尺寸均衡，暗示出既日用又可用于款待宾客的双重功能。

收藏历史方面，该酒杯曾为康涅狄格州斯坦福德的凯瑟琳·伊丽莎白·海文斯（Catherine Elizabeth Havens）所有，并由达德利·P·艾伦基金（Dudley P. Allen Fund）收藏于克利夫兰艺术博物馆装饰艺术与设计部，馆内编号为1934.378。此一背景信息增添了其历史流传脉络，使观者能更深入感受其文化价值。

观赏这件酒杯时，应重点关注其银质光泽和把手上的铭文，二者是了解其身份与历史的重要线索。同时，留意酒杯整体造型与工艺细节，它们体现了18世纪早期美国殖民手工艺的典型样式與精湛技艺。该器物不仅是实用器皿，更是历史与身份的象征，揭示了殖民地社会的工艺水准与文化特点。

This silver tankard, created around 1710, originates from Newport, Rhode Island, a significant American colonial center famous for its fine silversmithing in the 18th century. It was crafted by Samuel Vernon (1683–1737), a recognized American silversmith of the period. Measuring 20.7 cm in height and 21.8 cm in width including the handle, the tankard’s dimensions are typical for everyday use of the era.

The tankard is constructed entirely of silver, exemplifying the high craftsmanship of colonial American silversmiths. Its surface maintains the natural silver luster without additional painted decoration, reflecting the early 18th-century preference for material purity and understated elegance. An engraving on the top of the handle reads “H over I*H,” a detail that might indicate ownership, maker’s marks, or some form of personal or symbolic signature. While the precise meaning of this inscription remains uncertain, it offers significant documentary insight for understanding the context within which the object was used.

Structurally, the tankard features a robust handle designed for ease of grip and practical use. The connection between handle and body is solid and seamless, demonstrating a blend of functionality and aesthetics typical of the period. The craftsmanship reveals careful attention to finishing, with smooth contours and no visible imperfections, indicative of a skilled maker’s hand. The balanced proportions and weight suggest the tankard was intended for both daily consumption and perhaps social hospitality.

Regarding provenance, the tankard was once in the collection of Catherine Elizabeth Havens of Stamford, Connecticut. It is currently held by the Cleveland Museum of Art’s Department of Decorative Art and Design, under accession number 1934.378, acquired through the Dudley P. Allen Fund. This recorded ownership history enriches the artifact’s narrative by connecting it to specific individuals and institutions, providing further cultural context.

When viewing this tankard, attention should be paid to the inscription on the handle and the quality of the silver surface. These features are crucial for understanding its historical identity and the artisan’s signature. Likewise, the tankard’s overall form and craftsmanship details are key to appreciating the typology and aesthetics of early 18th-century American colonial silverwork. Far beyond a mere utilitarian vessel, this tankard embodies a material record of social identity and artistic skill during its period.

text:
Maria Ressa has been fighting this war longer than most people have known it exists.

Rappler, the Philippine investigative outlet she founded, has been under coordinated state-linked attack for years. Not theoretical pressure. Documented, systematic attack: bot networks amplifying false narratives, mass coordinated reporting campaigns designed to suppress Rappler content in platform algorithms, legal proceedings stacked up by the Duterte administration and its successors to impose costs and burn resources, and cross-border targeting as Ressa moved internationally. The full toolkit. Ressa won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021 and the harassment did not stop. If anything, the international attention added a transnational layer to what had already been a sophisticated domestic operation.

The Atlantic ran a feature on Rappler in October 2026 documenting something worth sitting with: after years of fighting on terrain controlled by corporate platforms, Rappler changed the terrain.

The piece frames this as a "digital commons" model, which is accurate enough, but the underlying logic is simpler and more important than the framing suggests. Rappler looked at the architecture of its own harassment and identified the structural vulnerability that state-linked actors were exploiting. That vulnerability was platform dependency. Facebook, in particular. And the solution was to stop organizing its public presence around infrastructure that its adversaries could manipulate.

This is not a radical insight in the abstract. But executing it is a different matter, and Rappler has done it in a threat environment that would have finished most outlets.

Here is the actual mechanism worth understanding. When a state-linked actor in the Philippines, or anywhere else, wants to suppress independent journalism on corporate social media, they have several reliable options. They can run coordinated inauthentic amplification to drown out the journalist's content with counter-narrative noise. They can organize mass reporting campaigns that trigger automated content moderation and algorithmic suppression without the platform ever having to make a deliberate editorial decision. They can purchase advertising that reaches the journalist's own audience with targeted disinformation. And they can do all of this at scale while the journalist and their organization are scrambling to keep the lights on, fight legal battles, and produce actual journalism.

Meta's documented and consistent failure to enforce its own coordinated inauthentic behavior policies in non-English language markets has been noted by Citizen Lab and other researchers for years. This is not a new complaint. The gap between Meta's stated policies and its enforcement reality in markets like the Philippines has been a known and exploitable vulnerability since at least the height of the Duterte administration's troll farm operations. State-linked actors in the Philippines understood this before most Western observers did, and they used it.

The platform, in this context, is not neutral infrastructure. It is a lever. And if your editorial survival depends on that platform, whoever controls the lever has meaningful power over you.

Rappler's response was to build toward what the Atlantic calls "platform sovereignty," which means direct audience relationships through owned channels, community infrastructure that exists independent of algorithmic decisions made in Menlo Park, and an archiving and documentation capability that does not disappear when a coordinated reporting campaign successfully removes content from a corporate platform. That last point is underappreciated. Corporate platform evidence of harassment campaigns vanishes constantly through content removal, account deletion, and platform-side decisions. An outlet with its own documentation infrastructure can maintain an evidentiary record that a platform-dependent outlet simply cannot.

None of this is a complete defense. Rappler still operates in a legal environment that has been weaponized against it. Ressa has faced multiple prosecutorial actions. The Philippine state's capacity for transnational harassment does not disappear because Rappler has a better website architecture. Platform sovereignty is a partial solution, not a total one.

But partial solutions matter when you are working in an environment where total solutions do not exist. What Rappler has done is close off one significant attack vector while retaining the capacity to document the others.

The broader pattern here is one I have watched develop across multiple regions and multiple threat environments. The state-sponsored harassment of independent media in the Philippines, in the MENA region, across Southeast Asia, across the former Soviet space, follows recognizable common architecture: legal weaponization, coordinated inauthentic amplification, platform manipulation, transnational targeting of journalists who travel internationally or have diaspora audiences. The tactics are adapted to local conditions but the underlying logic is consistent. And in almost every case, the journalists and outlets on the receiving end have organized their public presence around corporate platforms that their adversaries have demonstrated they can manipulate.

Rappler's evolution offers something practical for counter-interference practitioners and for the democratic governments and civil society organizations that fund independent media resilience programs. The question of how to support independent journalism in authoritarian-adjacent information environments has usually been answered in terms of legal support, security training, and journalism capacity. Those matter. But the structural question of platform dependency as a security vulnerability has received less systematic attention than it deserves.

If a state-linked actor can suppress an outlet's content by coordinating mass reports to a platform's automated moderation system, then that outlet's platform dependency is an information security problem, not just an editorial preference. The framing matters because it changes what kinds of support and investment make sense. Legal defense funds are important. So is the infrastructure investment required to build genuine platform independence.

The Rappler model is not easily replicated by every small independent outlet operating under similar threat conditions. Building a digital commons infrastructure requires resources, technical capacity, and an existing audience relationship substantial enough to sustain a transition away from platform-dependent distribution. Rappler has those things in part because of Ressa's international profile and the Nobel recognition that came with it. A smaller outlet in a less internationally visible threat environment does not automatically have the same starting position.

But the template exists now in a documented form, which is itself useful. And the underlying analysis, that platform sovereignty is a component of information security for independent media in state-sponsored harassment environments, is transferable even when the specific implementation has to be adapted.

I have been watching the toolkit that authoritarian and semi-authoritarian states use against independent journalism for long enough to notice when something actually shifts. Most of what I write about is the same playbook being run in new places against new targets. The Rappler story is genuinely something different, not because the harassment stopped, but because the target rebuilt its own architecture in response to a systematic analysis of how the harassment worked. That happens less often than it should.

text:
Ukraine is not hitting Russian refineries for fun. It is hitting them because those plants turn crude into diesel, jet fuel, and gasoline that keep Russian tanks, trucks, aircraft, and occupation logistics running.

A country that launched a full-scale war of aggression does not get a protected energy sector. Under the law of armed conflict, objects that make an effective contribution to military action and whose destruction offers a definite military advantage are military objectives. Refineries feeding the Russian war machine meet that test.

Russia has spent years striking Ukrainian power plants, substations, dams, ports, and heating systems in winter. Moscow does not get to demand immunity for its own fuel system while it tries to freeze and black out Ukrainian cities.

Diesel prices are a real political problem. They are not a legal veto. If higher pump prices were enough to outlaw strikes on an aggressor’s war fuel, every defender would have to fight with one hand tied so distant markets stayed comfortable.

Trump can ask Kyiv to spare refineries. That is a policy preference about inflation and talks. It is not a finding that the targets are illegitimate. Zelensky’s job is to degrade Russia’s ability to keep killing Ukrainians, not to manage global product balances for Washington.

If the United States wants those strikes to stop, the serious path is a real energy-for-energy halt: Russia stops hitting Ukrainian infrastructure, Ukraine pauses refinery strikes, with verification. Begging only Ukraine to stand down while Russia keeps firing is not neutrality. It is asking the victim to subsidize the invader’s fuel supply.

Ukraine has the right to hit the refineries that power the army occupying its land. That right does not disappear because diesel is expensive.

text:
WE COUNT THE ENEMIES WE KILL. WE RARELY COUNT THE ONES WE CREATE.

Nidal Hasan was a patient on my floor in the surgical trauma ICU at Brooke Army Medical Center.

I wasn't there when he arrived. I had just left for my deployment to Mosul, Iraq. But the nurses and doctors who cared for him were my peers and my friends, and I know exactly what that required of them, because every one of us had done some version of it before.  Before anyone tells me what strength looks like, understand what that work demands.

I have cared for a drunk driver who wiped out an entire family and landed in our ICU himself. I have cared for gang members who shot up a block while children were stepping off a school bus, then ended up on our unit with bullets of their own. I have kept alive people who murdered their own families and failed at taking their own lives. And in Iraq, I saved the lives of the very enemy fighters who had just tried to kill us and miraculously survived our response.

Every one of those patients got our best. Not because we felt anything for them, but because of who we were. You set aside anger, grief, prejudice and every personal feeling you have, because a life in front of you is a life in front of you. That's the oath. That's the duty.

So when Hasan came through those doors, my colleagues did what we had always done. They preserved the life of a man who murdered thirteen people and would have killed them too, given the chance. He killed those men and women in one of the very same buildings many Soldier's like myself have been in when I was stationed at Fort Hood.
He is alive today because they did their jobs. That was not sentiment. It was a hard, tangible expression of the values this country claims to stand for. Our principles had to mean something even when the person benefiting from them had violated everything we believed in.

Now the Pentagon plans to livestream his execution by firing squad on Dec. 3, and our leaders apparently believe turning his death into a public spectacle will demonstrate American strength. I think it demonstrates how little they understand the enemy they claim to be fighting. We kept Nidal Hasan alive, now our leaders want to make him a martyr.

Hasan walked into Fort Hood expecting to die. He believed his death would be rewarded. At his trial, he called no witnesses and offered no defense, and his own court-appointed lawyers worried he was seeking execution. He failed at martyrdom once. Now we're about to hand it to him, in high definition, for every extremist with an internet connection to replay, manipulate and celebrate.
We supply the footage. They supply the meaning.
Long after the politicians finish congratulating themselves, that video will still exist. Their moment of bravado becomes somebody else's recruiting material for decades.  And this failure to think past the immediate display of power reaches far beyond one execution.  We count the enemies we kill. We rarely count the enemies we create.

Look at the school in Minab, Iran, where multiple investigations attributed the strike that killed more than 100 children and their teachers to us. You cannot bury people's children beneath the rubble of their classrooms and expect a speech about American intentions to decide how they remember you.  No denial brings those children home. No claim of good intentions makes their parents forget whose weapons killed them.
If those were our children, we would remember for the rest of our lives. We would demand accountability. Many of us would want vengeance. We would tell their stories to the next generation. We know this because we did exactly that after September 11.

Why do we imagine other people love their children less, grieve less deeply, or remember less clearly?

We have developed a horrifying talent for creating more terrorists than we will ever stop. We inflict suffering, evade responsibility, and then act as though the anger that follows came out of nowhere.
