text:
The Twelve Months Sanctified by Prayer: October, Month of the Holy Angels M. L'ABBE A. RICARD, D.S.G. Translated from the French. 1877 October 26 DEVOTION TO OUR ANGEL-GUARDIAN.
.
Prelude.
.
Our angel-guardian watches at our side, and sees all our proceedings and our wants.
.
Meditation.
.
It would indeed be very difficult to help having a particular devotion to our good angel-guardians, for we should need to have neither intelligence nor heart not to feel an entire and perfect gratitude towards them. Let us honour very much all angel-guardians, and first of all those of infidels, and let us go in spirit to converse with them, keep them company, and express our regrets for the infidelity of the souls they guard, and who do not even know of their presence at their side. Let us do the same for the angel-guardians of heretics and poor ignorant beings, who have no more light about the holy angels than those who live in the midst of infidel lands. Let us venerate and love the angel-guardians of our friends; they render us on many occasions great services, and as demons strive to unite bad friendships, so the holy angels omit nothing to unite together persons who give themselves to God. Let us pray to the good angels of our spiritual directors, so that they may inspire them with pure counsels, conformed to the Divine Will. Let us also offer our homage to the angel guardians of our parents, of persons with whom we may have business, of our benefactors, because it was their holy angels who inspired them to help us; of our enemies, that they may bless their hearts. Let us venerate equally the angel-guardians of kingdoms, provinces, towns, and villages, where we live, or through which we pass. It is also a holy practice to implore the aid of the angels of the diocese in which we are, of the prelate who governs it, and of his co-operators, so that they may obtain the establishment of the reign of Jesus Christ in the faithful who are subject to them, the destruction of the empire of Satan, and also the necessary light to govern the diocese holily.
.
Resolution.
.
Renew our devotion to the holy angel-guardians.
.
Aspiration.
.
"Holy angel-guardians, pray for us." (Litany of the Holy Angels)
.
Example: The Angel of the  Crusades.
.
Cardinal Baronius (1146) thought it was an angel who saved the array of Crusaders on the occasion of which I am going to speak, and it was also the opinion of William of Tyre, as his narrative insinuates (Book xvi. ch. xii. and xiii). And, in reality, the event cannot be explained in any other way. The Crusaders had advanced into the enemy's country, and found themselves in such an awkward position that no safety was left them except by retreat; but to escape from the Saracens, who had blocked the roads, it was necessary to know the by-ways, and they had no guide at their disposition. However, the army began its march, and immediately at the head of the vanguard was seen an unknown knight, mounted on a white horse, encased in brilliant armour, and holding a red banner in his hand. He conducted them by short paths, where they found water in abundance, pointed out the best places for encampment, and conducted them in three days to Gadara, which, without him, they could not have attained in five days' march. What finally proves that it was an angel, was, that he disappeared every evening, for he could never be found in the camp, and reappeared in the morning at the hour of departure. The army was saved by him from an almost certain ruin.
.
Holland, September 29

text:
John continues:

'I was sent back to Ilfracombe for an NCO course. By this time, there were a large number of very experienced soldiers of the French Foreign Legion stationed in Ilfracombe. They were tough guys and refused to take orders.

Being on guard duty one night, I walked past the side of the Osborne Hotel and heard a noise coming from an upstairs window. Although it was black-out, I saw two French Foreign Legion soldiers coming out of an upstairs window, one with a bar in his hand, and trying to climb onto a corrugated roof.

My guard commander, Sergeant Heinrich, challenged him and both men were subsequently sentenced to a period of army detention in Shepton Mallet in Somerset.

Sergeant Passmore, irregular army sergeant, and myself had the misfortune of taking the two soldiers to the detention barracks.

Whilst changing trains at Taunton, a lady felt sorry for us and offered the four of us a cup of tea in the cafe, not realising that the two men were handcuffed to us. When these two soldiers were eventually released from detention, they returned to Ilfracombe

One evening I was standing at the bar of a pub near the harbour and these two soldiers walked up behind me, lifted me up and threw me into the harbour - not realising that I was not a good swimmer. Even so, I did not press charges - I did not want to escort them back to Shepton Mallet.

I later attended an NCO course at Woolacombe where I gained my first experience of live ammunition.

We were taken out into the sea and our boats were turned over. We had to swim back to shore making quite certain that our guns did not get wet.

Not an easy task.

This was the summer of 1941.

After this training, I was promoted to Sergeant.’

(continued)

authorBio: Author & Historian of 25+ books on WWII, espionage & spies. Expert on Secret Listeners, Germans who fought for Britain, and Women in Intelligence Services.

text:
John continues:

'Sergeant Hill had said ‘Visolet?’

His foreign accent had obscured the English which was supposed to be: ‘why are you so late?’ and I had replied, ‘no, thank you.’

The charge was dropped and after a few weeks of training in Ilfracombe I was promoted to Lord Reading’s Stick-guard. I had to walk behind him with a stick.

Everywhere he went in Ilfracombe, I followed.

Whilst training in Ilfracombe, I walked through the army quarters and I saw a few men forming an army band.

There was a violinist who was having difficulty tuning his violin. As a child, I had had a number of violin lessons but gave up because I had no musical talent. I offered to tune his violin.

At that moment our Commanding Officer saw what I was doing and commanded me to become the band leader. So as not to disappoint, I learnt to play the signature tune which was “Sweet Sue”.

Once the band had formed, we played in all the officers’ mess as well as for the local WRNS and ATS.

We earned a few shillings each night.

We were excused all fatigue jobs in the day, like peeling potatoes. We had no drum kit in the band, so we used a tea chest and shoe brushes.     

After Ilfracombe, I was posted to Avonmouth where our company was stationed for around 90 days. At the end of this, I was promoted to Lance Corporal or Corporal.'

(continued)

text:
WEEKEND MUSINGS:

ASABA MASSACRE: 59 YEARS ON, THE WOUNDS STILL BLEED — A NATION CANNOT HEAL BY PRETENDING TO FORGET

On 7 October 1967, during the Nigerian Civil War, Asaba witnessed one of the darkest and most devastating genocide in human history. Fifty-nine years later, the tears may have dried on some faces, but the wounds remain painfully alive in the memory of a people whose innocence was shattered by unimaginable cruelty.

They were not soldiers confronting an advancing army on the battlefield. They were ordinary, unarmed civilians—fathers, sons, brothers, young men, women and children, who came out in the hope that peace had finally returned. Some gathered in a procession, trusting that the arrival of Federal troops meant the restoration of peace and normalcy. Instead, men and boys were separated from their loved ones and brutally executed. Hundreds perished; historical estimates vary, but the enormity of the tragedy is beyond dispute.

Imagine a mother watching her husband and sons walk away, believing they would return, only to wait in vain. Imagine children growing up without fathers, wives condemned to widowhood, and families left to mourn loved ones whose lives were extinguished without mercy. Imagine a community forced to bury not merely its dead, but its hopes, dreams and sense of security.

The Asaba Massacre was not merely a tragedy of 1967; it was a wound inflicted upon the conscience of a nation.

Someone gave orders; others executed them. The precise chain of individual responsibility must be judged against the historical evidence. Yet, no dispute over the past should diminish the undeniable suffering of the victims or the moral obligation of the Nigerian state to acknowledge this atrocity.

Today, in the spirit of forgiveness and reconciliation, and in keeping with the declaration of “No Victor, No Vanquished” at the end of the Civil War, the people of Asaba are asking for something neither extravagant nor unreasonable: an unqualified public apology from a sitting President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria.

Through their revered traditional ruler, the Asagba of Asaba, HRM Prof. Epiphany Azinge, SAN, the community has made its position unmistakably clear: there can be no genuine closure or complete healing until a serving President publicly apologises for the massacre. General Yakubu Gowon has apologised in retirement, but the community seeks the solemn acknowledgement of the Nigerian state through its incumbent President.

Consider the national recognition accorded to Chief Moshood Kashimawo Olawale Abiola and the official recognition of 12 June as Democracy Day in honour of his struggle for democratic governance. If Nigeria can acknowledge historical injustice and immortalise a defining chapter in its democratic journey, why should a formal presidential apology to the innocent victims of Asaba be beyond reach?

The demand is not for revenge. It is a plea for truth, dignity and recognition. It is a call for the nation to look its painful history in the face and acknowledge the humanity of those whose lives were so cruelly cut short.

As an African proverb reminds us, “Until the lion learns to write, every story will glorify the hunter.” The story of Asaba must never be buried beneath the convenience of silence or the passage of time.

We cannot continue to move forward as though nothing happened. The greatest injustice to the dead and the living is to pretend that all is well when an unhealed wound continues to trouble the conscience of an entire community. Forgiveness may be offered, but it must never be demanded as a substitute for acknowledgement; reconciliation must not become another name for forgetting.

Asaba remembers its fallen sons and daughters. Nigeria must remember them, too. Their blood was shed on Nigerian soil, and their memory belongs to the history of our common nation.

Mr President, the people of Asaba are not asking you to rewrite history. They are asking you to acknowledge it. An unqualified presidential apology would not restore the dead, erase the trauma or undo the devastation of 1967. But it would affirm that their lives mattered, that their suffering has not been forgotten, and that the Nigerian state recognises its moral obligation to the bereaved community.

Let the government heed the counsel of the Asagba of Asaba. Let the nation choose the courage of acknowledgement over the comfort of silence.

May the souls of the innocent victims continue to rest in peace, and may their memory remain a solemn reminder that no national unity is worth the deliberate destruction of innocent lives.

“There will be no closure, there will be no healing until a sitting President—not an ex-President, but a sitting President—publicly apologises to us.”

— HRM Prof. Epiphany Azinge, SAN, Asagba of Asaba

From the going down of the sun until the morning, we shall remember them. May their memory never fade, and may justice, at last, find its voice.

Signed:

Sir Ifeanyi Ejiofor, Esq. (KSC)
Dunu-Ezeugosinachi
10 October 2026

Daily UK defence and security brief from Think Defence, Saturday 10 October 2026, covering the previous 24 hours.

NEWS

Latvian Men Arrested at RAF Molesworth Released on Bail

Two Latvian men, aged 32 and 26 and resident in the UK, have been released on bail with strict conditions after being found inside RAF Molesworth, the Cambridgeshire base used by US and NATO intelligence operations including NATO's Intelligence Fusion Centre. They were arrested early on Thursday after MoD Police found an abandoned vehicle and a small fence breach, initially on suspicion of trespass and criminal damage and then under Section 4 of the National Security Act; Counter Terrorism Policing London said the investigation continues and there is so far no link to the RAF Fairford incident.

The Guardian
https://t.co/CoXBauLjIW

Trump Announces Russian Diesel Deal as Zelensky Calls It a Gift to Putin

President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned Donald Trump's announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel into the US, calling it a gift to Vladimir Putin and an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. Trump said Putin had agreed to release hundreds of thousands of tonnes of diesel to American and global markets, with the US Treasury understood to be suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April; a UK government spokesperson said Britain would keep supporting Ukraine and maintain pressure on Russia through sanctions.

BBC
https://t.co/DNnCaNVicE

Yandex Struggles After Ukrainian Drone Strikes on Russian Data Centres

Russian tech group Yandex said it was struggling to keep services running after Ukrainian drones struck two of its five data centres, at Sasovo in the Ryazan region and in Kaluga, in what President Zelensky described as a mirror response to Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centres. Ukraine's defence ministry said the strikes could force Russia to divert resources to repairs; Yandex, often dubbed Russia's Google, said operations at Sasovo were completely suspended and parts of the Kaluga site were out of service.

BBC
https://t.co/smIimDiTNr

UK Joins Allies Opposing US Sanctions on the International Criminal Court

The Trump administration unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court as an institution, including curbs on US entities dealing with it, which the court called an assault on the rule of law. The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in reaffirming unwavering support for the ICC and saying they regret and strongly disagree with the sanctions, hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize.

BBC
https://t.co/5dy5zrdRlG

Pro-Kremlin Rybar Blogger Arrested in Montenegro

Montenegrin authorities detained Mikhail Zvinchuk, founder of the influential pro-Kremlin Rybar military blog, with his wife and three other Russians in the Adriatic town of Risan on suspicion of spreading Russian influence, after warnings of hybrid warfare attempts. Prime Minister Milojko Spajić confirmed the detention; local media later reported the group was to be expelled on national security grounds, while Rybar said Russia's foreign ministry was engaged and expected release.

The Guardian
https://t.co/kR8LPMw9hs

UK Coastguard Chief Faces Calls to Resign Over Misleading Pay Claims

Maritime and Coastguard Agency chief executive Virginia McVea faces resignation calls after the Office for Statistics Regulation found agency survey data did not sufficiently support her claim that more than 90% of coastguard rescue officers backed a plan to stop remunerating them. The GMB union and MPs said she had misled coastguards and parliamentarians in a pay row that followed a court ruling affirming rescue officers' worker status; it is understood the option of ending pay is no longer on the table.

The Guardian
https://t.co/nMuVhv1or3

Conservatives Pledge £10 Billion Britannia Shield Air Defence Network

Shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge told the Conservative conference the party would allocate up to £10 billion over ten years for Britannia Shield, an integrated air-and-missile defence system built around sense, decide and effect layers including radars, upgraded command and control, interceptors, counter-UAV capability and larger missile stockpiles. Jane's reports the plan emphasises rapid delivery from existing equipment, with a minimum deployable capability in a first term and possible assignment to sovereign base areas in Cyprus and the Falkland Islands.

Jane's

Wiltshire-based Avon Protection has secured a US Department of War order for its MITR-M1 half mask, MITR-PG1 powered goggles and related particulate and riot filters, its second MITR customer this year after Canada. President Steve Elwell said the award followed nearly four years of collaborative development; the lighter system is designed to be worn with a helmet and communications kit and offers protection against common CBRN threats including riot agents, smoke and biological agents.

Calibre Defence

Commodore David Burton told the Apex Europe conference in London that Britain is lead nation for NATO's Allied Underwater Battlespace Mission Network, binding frigates, uncrewed underwater and surface vehicles, sensors and satellite links into an interoperable undersea domain-awareness network he described as the alliance's most significant such initiative since the Cold War. Twelve nations sponsor the programme, with a second phase worth more than £30 million to build a test and reference environment through 2028, and British industry involved via the Mangrove consortium including Saab UK, BlueBear and S2IX.

The company, owned equally by BAE Systems, Leonardo and Japan's JAIEC, said the site will sustain thousands of skilled engineering jobs in the region as GCAP advances through concept and assessment towards design and development, with an in-service target of 2035 replacing Typhoon in RAF service.

text:
India Needs Its Own Digital Ecosystem 

Recent global tech disputes have highlighted a critical reality: excessive dependence on foreign digital platforms can leave India vulnerable to decisions that may not align with its national interests.

India has no shortage of engineering talent. Our developers and innovators power some of the world’s biggest technology companies. Yet, when it comes to social media and digital platforms, we still rely heavily on services built and controlled overseas.

China offers one example of how domestic platforms such as WeChat and Weibo can help build a strong local technology ecosystem. India can draw lessons from this approach while developing its own model—one rooted in innovation, openness, privacy and accountability.

We need homegrown social media platforms that can compete globally, protect users’ data under Indian law, and ensure that decisions affecting our public discourse are not solely in the hands of foreign corporations.

Digital sovereignty is more than a technology goal. It is an economic and strategic priority.

India has the talent, market and ambition to build world-class digital platforms. The next step is to turn that potential into products that Indians can trust—and the world can use.

The goal should not simply be to replace foreign platforms, but to build better alternatives that succeed on merit, security and user trust.

text:
Stanley Kubrick died six days after delivering his final cut of Eyes Wide Shut to Warner Bros. He was seventy years old. His heart gave out, they said. The timing has haunted people ever since, and not without reason. 
 Because what Kubrick put on screen in 1999 was not, as the press claimed, an erotic thriller about a jealous husband and a wandering wife. It was something far more dangerous: a portrait of how the ultra-wealthy have always operated in the shadows, and what happens to the young women who get caught in that world.
 Jeffrey Epstein made the subtext impossible to ignore.
 A Story That Predates Epstein by a Century
 Here is the first thing you need to know: Kubrick did not invent this story. Eyes Wide Shut is based on Arthur Schnitzler’s 1926 novella, Traumnovelle, or Dream Story, a work Kubrick optioned in 1970 and spent nearly three decades developing. The novella already contained a masked s*x party, a woman sacrificed to protect an intruder, and a costume shop owner who offers his teenage daughter for s*x. Schnitzler was writing about the Viennese upper class before World War One. The s*xual predation of the powerful was not a new story in 1926. It was not a new story in 1999. And Kubrick knew it.
 That is precisely why the source material drew him in for thirty years. Not because it was salacious. Because it was true.
 What Kubrick Actually Built
 Kubrick was not a journalist. He did not have a list of names. But he was among the most precise and obsessive filmmakers who ever lived, a man who personally selected every mask worn during the orgy sequence, who chose the Venetian carnival aesthetic to evoke centuries of aristocratic anonymity, who shot the ritual scene at Mentmore Towers, a nineteenth-century English estate built for the Rothschild family.
 Nothing in a Kubrick film is accidental
 The world he constructed in Eyes Wide Shut is one where a physician, Bill Harford, exists on the edge of real power without understanding it. He is educated, respected, comfortable. He knows rich people. He thinks he is close to the center of things. Then his wife Alice, in a moment of unsettling honesty, tells him she once came close to destroying their marriage for a man she barely knew, and something cracks open in him.
 What follows is less a plot than an initiation. Bill stumbles into a world that has always existed around him, one of masked ceremonies, of women who appear and disappear without explanation, of a power structure that can threaten a man into silence with a single unmasking. When he finally confronts Victor Ziegler, the wealthy patron who connects his two worlds, Ziegler explains it to him with calm contempt: the woman who sacrificed herself to save Bill was already gone. The whole thing was theater, Ziegler says. Or maybe it wasn’t. The point is that Bill will never know. And that is how it is supposed to work.
 Scholar Arthur Versluis describes this as political gnosis, a revelation that behind the wealth and glamor of the American elite lies initiation into a corrupted secret network. He specifically notes the film’s depiction of human trafficking, of young women used for s*xual exploitation by men who face no consequences because their money insulates them from accountability. The film does not show underage girls. It does not need to. The structure it reveals is the same structure.
 The Epstein Mirror
 In July 2019, Jeffrey Epstein was arrested on federal s*x trafficking charges. He had spent decades running a network that funneled young girls, many of them minors, to the most powerful men in the world. He had already been convicted once, in 2008, and received a sentence so lenient it became a national scandal in itself. 
 He had connections to presidents, princes, tech billionaires, financiers, and celebrities. He owned an island. He owned a private jet. He had a house in New York, a compound in New Mexico, a flat in Paris, and a townhouse in Manhattan that was one of the largest private residences in the city.
 He was found dead in his cell in August 2019. The official ruling was su*cide. Not everyone believes it.
 When Newsweek and other major outlets began directly comparing Eyes Wide Shut to the Epstein case, they were not reaching. The architecture of the film maps almost perfectly onto what Epstein ran. A wealthy gatekeeper who controls access. Young women provided to powerful men. A world sealed off from ordinary scrutiny by money, by legal protection, by the threat of ruin to anyone who talks. And at the center of it all, not some cartoonish villain but men who move through polite society, who attend charity galas and shake hands with politicians, whose public lives are defined by philanthropy and prestige.
 Bill Harford is any of us who got close enough to glimpse it and then was sent home.
 The Pattern Is Ancient
 The exploitation of young women by wealthy and powerful men is not a modern invention. It is not even a feature of capitalism specifically, though capitalism has refined and institutionalized it. It runs through every civilization with a ruling class. Roman senators. Medieval lords. Nineteenth-century industrialists who kept chorus girls and factory workers in parallel forms of bondage. The Viennese bourgeoisie Schnitzler wrote about in 1926. The Manhattan financiers Kubrick updated them into in 1999.
 What Kubrick understood, and what the Epstein scandal confirmed with brutal clarity, is that the mechanism is always the same. Money creates access. Access creates opportunity. Power creates silence. The young women who enter that world are rarely there by genuine choice. They are there because poverty, ambition, coercion, or predatory grooming put them there. And when something goes wrong, the weight of the entire structure comes down to protect the men at the top.
 The girl in Eyes Wide Shut who “redeems” Bill at the orgy, who offers herself in his place, who turns up dead afterward in circumstances that are never explained: she is not an abstraction. She is every young woman who entered Epstein’s orbit and found that the price of the world she was being shown was her body and her silence.
 What the Film Cannot Say
 Kubrick made a film about this world, but he made it as a dream. The title itself signals the condition he was diagnosing. Eyes wide shut. We are standing in front of it. We can see it, if we choose to see it. Most of us choose not to.
 The orgy scene at Mentmore Towers is choreographed to feel both specific and unreal. The masks create anonymity. The ceremony has weight and ritual, the passwords, the central authority figure, the slow procession of participants. But it is also lit and staged to feel slightly wrong, like a memory or a hallucination. Kubrick gave himself and his audience plausible deniability. This is a dream, the film suggests. This is a man’s paranoid projection. Perhaps none of it really happened.
 That ambiguity was both artistically honest and strategically necessary. A film that claimed to directly document elite s*x trafficking in 1999 would never have been made, distributed, or seen. Kubrick found a way to tell the truth by wrapping it in enough unreality that no one could sue him for it.
 He finished it. He died. Warner Bros. digitally obscured parts of the orgy scene for the American theatrical release without his approval, a decision that Roger Ebert and other critics found indefensible. The cuts were made to avoid an NC-17 rating, officially. Draw your own conclusions.
 Seeing It Clearly Now
 The Epstein case did not change what Kubrick made. It changed what we are able to see in it.
 Eyes Wide Shut is a film about the oldest racket in the world: the powerful taking what they want from the young and the vulnerable, shielded by wealth, by ritual, by the complicity of everyone around them who understands the rules and stays quiet. Schnitzler saw it in Vienna in 1926. Kubrick saw it in New York in 1999. It took us until 2019, until an island and a flight log and a dead man in a Manhattan jail cell, to see it as clearly as they did.
 It was never a conspiracy theory. It was always just reality.
 And the title was always the point. Eyes wide shut. That is not an accusation aimed at the powerful. It is aimed at the rest of us.
 ---

Nik Storonsky outlines Revolut’s ambition to become a global tech company beyond banking by 2034.

Speaking at Wave by Vento in Torino, the Revolut CEO said the goal is to build a business of similar scale to Meta, Google, Anthropic or OpenAI — but from Europe — and “not be only in banking, but also in other services, technology services that enhance people’s lives.” By 2034, Revolut should be “a much bigger part of our lives and helping us with many more things than just banking or financial services.”

Revolut is already building proprietary models such as Pragma, trained on its transactional data. “We have thirty, forty million of transactions happening every day,” Storonsky noted, and the company is constructing its own data centres to train them.

Near-term AI plans include shopping capabilities: users tell AI by Revolut (AIR) what to buy, it browses stores and purchases securely with stored card details. The same system will offer financial analytics and advice on stocks, funds and personal finances — effectively “your own kind of financial system, which can buy things, invest in things, advise you on your financial life.”

Revolut also intends to open its platform so third-party AI agents can interact with its own via MCPs (with customer authentication). Storonsky prefers this open approach over a closed ecosystem.

His comments signal a shift: Revolut is using AI, proprietary data and models to expand well beyond core banking into broader everyday services, aiming to compete at the scale of the largest global tech companies by its 20th year.

text:
❯ Demoscene: Blackout State by Darklite

Every demo comes with a small text file, and most of them say who did what and whom they greet. The one beside Blackout State, winner of the newschool demo competition at Black Valley 2026, has a line near the top that reads like a dare:

API...........: Pure OpenGL (Strictly NO SHADERS used!)

The tech notes further down agree: "Pure OpenGL. Zero shaders. Everything you see is driven by oldschool pipeline rendering and raw math."

Watch it first, and mind the epilepsy warning, which it has earned honestly: https://t.co/yDDBg6IuEp

■ THREE NAMES ON THE NFO

Darklite is a Norwegian group based around Dokka, a small township in the east of the country. Rudi wrote the code and added graphics of his own. Phobium wrote the music, and tFt drew the graphics and the overlays.

Rudi's page on Demozoo explains why the NFO line is a choice made with open eyes: ninety-nine productions since 1998, and lately a run of MS-DOS intros of 256 bytes each, one of them a voxel engine. A man who can fit a landscape into fewer bytes than this paragraph has characters knows precisely what a modern graphics card offers, and in July he sat down and declined most of it.

■ THE CONSTRAINT IS A PIPELINE

In the first years of consumer 3D cards, the card was a machine with a fixed sequence of stages. Vertices went in, were transformed by a matrix and lit by a small set of lights with fixed equations, then textured, fogged, blended and written to the screen, and the programmer's part was to set switches and feed it triangles.

Shaders ended that. A shader is a small program the card runs for every vertex or every pixel, and once OpenGL took on its shading language with version 2.0 in 2004, the lighting and nearly everything after it became code the demo writes for itself. OpenGL 3.0 declared the fixed pipeline deprecated in 2008, and 3.1 took it out of the core specification. It survives in the compatibility profile, though few productions open that drawer any more, which is why wbcbz7 on Pouët handed out bonus props for going no-shaders.

I read the party version to see whether the NFO tells the truth. The file names seventy-one OpenGL functions, and they read like a manual from about 2001: glBegin and glEnd to send geometry one vertex at a time, glLightfv for the fixed lights, glMaterialfv for surfaces, glTexGeni to let the card generate texture coordinates, glCopyTexSubImage2D to copy the screen into a texture. Not one of the seventy-one compiles a shader, and the word does not appear anywhere in the sixty-million-byte file.

A graphics programmer will point out, quite rightly, that the card on their desk has no fixed lights left in it. The driver translates the old switches into a shader of its own, and in Mesa the file that does so opens with "Create a vertex program to execute the current fixed function T&L pipeline." The restriction binds the author and nobody else, which is where the scene has always put its restrictions: a 256-byte intro runs on a machine with megabytes to spare, and the bytes still count.

rloaderro on Pouët put the result in a sentence: "the meta envblobs with radial blur look ace. Cool idea to do a no-shaders, but with a lot more fillrate than what was available back in the days." The techniques are the ones people used when fill rate was the scarcest thing on the card, now running on hardware with vastly more of it, so an effect that once had to stay small can cover the screen and do it again on top of itself.

The essay has what else the file gives away about its builder, down to a greetings effect whose name suggests a certain green film.

■ ACID

Phobium's soundtrack is acid, and Pouët noticed. Kuemmel liked the evolution of that acid tune, PRiDE gave the soundtrack an exclamation mark of its own, rloaderro opened with "Norsk flagg acid!", which I take to be the highest praise available in the genre, and HellMood reported that it works great in his home cinema. An acid line is a small, deliberately limited synthesiser pushed as hard as it will go, and the pictures do the same with the pipeline.

■ BLACK VALLEY

Black Valley 2026 ran from 10 to 12 July at Blaker Samfunnshus, the community hall in Blaker near Lillestrøm, east of Oslo, organised by Menace with a team of fourteen. Among its competitions was one for Bossa Nova, which I would very much like to have heard. Five demos went up in newschool, and the hall voted:

Blackout State, Darklite, 182 points
Blaker Breeze, Skuggemannen and oklien, 161
Urban Cycles, Arctic Robots, 139
Don't Send It to Anyone, NoCMP, 101
Natural, +, 98

Twenty-one points clear of a production named after the village the party stood in, which at that party is no small thing.

■ WHAT THE PIPELINE STILL KNOWS

Darklite took the method of that era, its fixed lights, its vertices sent one at a time, its generated texture coordinates and its copied screens, and gave it the fill rate of a machine from this decade, to find out what the old way of drawing looks like when nothing is holding it back.

The NFO greets thirty-eight groups and signs its logo with a motto that suits the result rather well: we do not grow up.

✈️ The Royal Air Force has taken over Coventry's Broadgate for a huge free event this weekend, complete with a Typhoon aircraft experience, military working dogs and plenty of activities for the whole family!

The RAF Show arrived in Coventry city centre on Friday and will remain in Broadgate until Sunday 11 October, giving residents a rare opportunity to get up close to military aviation technology and meet some of the people who work in the Royal Air Force.

One of the biggest attractions is the RAF Typhoon display, where visitors can step inside and learn more about one of Britain's most recognisable fighter aircraft.

There will also be demonstrations involving military working dogs, virtual reality experiences, interactive science and engineering activities, and live performances from RAF musicians.

Visitors can also watch RAF chefs preparing food, try some samples and speak directly to serving personnel about their experiences. There are activities designed for children and adults, so you don't need to have any particular interest in joining the military to enjoy what's on offer.

It's not every weekend that Broadgate hosts something quite like this, and with so many families looking for affordable things to do around Coventry, it's particularly nice that the entire event is free.

The show is also a chance for younger visitors to discover more about engineering, technology and aviation, with plenty of hands-on activities rather than simply looking at displays.

📍 Location: Broadgate Square, Coventry city centre, CV1 1NF.
📅 Saturday 10 and Sunday 11 October.
🕙 Opening times: 10am–4.30pm both days.
🎟️ Admission: Completely FREE. No ticket or advance booking required.

text:
For the next two weeks, we argued about everything. The lease, the furniture, the flights I could afford to take home, and whether we should even bother trying long distance.

I kept saying I wanted him to support my dreams the way I'd supported his.

He finally reminded me that I'd supported his dream right up until it required me to make a sacrifice.

That shut me up.

He didn't ask me to reject the job. He didn't threaten to leave. He simply told me he couldn't promise he'd still be waiting for me when I came back.

I'm moving to Seattle next month.

Yesterday, I found the old email where he'd declined the Denver offer. He'd written that he was grateful for the opportunity but had decided to remain in Ohio for personal reasons.

I read it twice.

Then I realized that while I'd been telling myself he chose me, I'd never really considered what it cost him to do that.

He's still here, looking for another job. I'm still packing.

And the man I once called the love of my life now feels like someone whose future I was happy to sacrifice as long as I never had to sacrifice my own.

text:
I begged my boyfriend to turn down his dream job because I didn't want a long-distance relationship. Six months later, I accepted a job in another state without even asking him how he felt about it.

When Aaron got the offer, he was so excited he called me from the parking lot. He'd been trying to get that position for almost two years, and it meant moving from Ohio to Denver.

I cried when he told me. Not because I wasn't happy for him, but because we'd just signed a new lease, and I'd imagined us getting married within the next year.

I told him I couldn't do long distance. I said I didn't want to spend my twenties waiting for someone to come home on weekends.

He turned the job down.

I promised him we'd find another opportunity eventually. He said he was choosing us.

I thought that was the most romantic thing anyone had ever done for me.

text:
[TL;DR]
My approach to tithing ranges from disaster relief to funding open-source projects like @Redot_Engine, which I use to help teach young people programming, robotics, and engineering. The goal is to stop infantilizing the next generation, challenge them with meaningful work, and equip them to build productive, independent lives.

[WALL OF TEXT]
I've mentioned this before, but I take a somewhat nuanced approach to tithing.

Sometimes that means dropping everything, breaking out the "boys and their toys," and deploying our equipment and resources when SHTF and the local community needs help.

Other times, it means funding Redot, an open-source game engine.

You might be wondering, "How does LTG IV conflate disaster relief and funding a video game engine?"

Well, dear reader, I'm glad you asked! 🤗

I've long believed video games are an excellent springboard into much more complicated engineering disciplines.

There's a sweet spot between beginner-friendly tools like Scratch and throwing someone into the deep end with SDL, fbdev, or low-level programming (ask me how I know).

Redot occupies that middle ground beautifully. It's approachable enough to get someone building something interesting quickly, but sophisticated enough to gradually introduce electronics, networking, physics, robotics, and systems engineering. AI makes that learning curve even more approachable.

Some of you might remember my article about modifying a Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles arcade cabinet.

What started as a personal project became an elaborate exercise in electronics, power distribution, virtualization, and hardware integration. I'm still working on further modifications involving 3D printing, hypervisors, SPICE, multiple displays, and low-latency remote controls, concepts that overlap with my robotics and teleoperations work.

To the casual observer, it's a scaled TMNT arcade cabinet.

To me, it's an engineering curriculum hiding inside a video game.

And that's precisely my point.

I've had families from Church use my articles to introduce their children to electronics and programming. After visiting @wwwLiveFarm, some of their kids spent the entire car ride home asking their parents why school isn't like this.

YEAH, WHY ISN'T IT?!

I homeschool my own son, and having found formal education painfully boring myself, I have strong opinions about how we teach young people.

I also work with charitable organizations here in Texas helping homeless and vulnerable teenagers get fed, clothed, housed where possible, and educated.

One point I push particularly hard: We need to stop infantilizing teenagers.

Give them meat and potatoes. Difficult problems. Real tools. Meaningful responsibilities. Opportunities to fail, learn, and try again.

Most importantly, give them somebody willing to sit down and explain the complicated parts instead of watering everything down until there's nothing substantial left to learn.

That's why I spend my free time writing technical articles and developing curricula, and why I find Redot so useful (and fund it when I can, and as I rotate tithing around trying to douse the biggest fire at the moment).

The objective isn't necessarily to produce video game developers. It's to give young people an approachable entry point into increasingly sophisticated subjects, then help them progress toward apprenticeships, skilled trades, university, or employment.

We're already doing this at @wwwLiveFarm.

This summer, my university interns explored some of my arcade and systems engineering work. We didn't have enough time to connect everything, but we did get our autonomous rover prototype out onto a public road, with the interns controlling it using an Xbox controller while we followed behind.

Suddenly, networking, latency, radio communications, and systems integration weren't abstract concepts anymore.

They were driving an actual robot on a public road while we drove behind it with neighbors staring and some even stopping us to ask us what on Earth we are doing.

Several of those interns have since received full-time aerospace job offers based on their engineering work at @wwwLiveFarm over the summer.

A number would also like to return as full-time engineers, but we're still bootstrapping and self-funding everything, so we simply can't afford that yet.

If I can't afford to hire somebody, the least I can do is help prepare them for someone who can.

And the interest keeps growing. Just this past Thursday night in Dallas, I had additional University of Texas students asking about interning with us. I told them yes. Now we'll have four universities under our banner:

• MIT
• Texas A&M
• University of Texas
• Purdue

Young Americans are hungry for opportunities to do meaningful work. We should be giving them those opportunities instead of squelching their opportunities in favor of foreigners and denigrating our young compatriots.

Which brings me back to Redot and tithing.

When I financially support an open-source project, I'm helping maintain a tool I can use to teach children from Church, homeless teenagers, university interns, and others who might otherwise never encounter this kind of engineering.

And because it's open source, they can take those tools and that knowledge with them, continue learning, and build something of their own. They don't need me for this; I'm just knocking over dominoes to get a chain reaction started.

I don't particularly care whether they eventually work for @wwwLiveFarm (obviously this is what I'd prefer), an aerospace company, a machine shop, or start their own business, so long as they GGGOOO!!! My wife and I have friends in from Dubai right now, and their tribe's language is Batak from the island of Sumatra. When we were grocery shopping tonight, they told me their nickname for me is "hatop" which means "hurry" because I'm always bugging out and screaming "Code 3!" (lights and sirens), or when I'm really getting frustrated, "JUST F'N GO!!!" since I'm pressed for time and trying to get us all moved on from one point to the next with as little time as possible in between. Okay, I guess I can take that as a compliment. 😂

In essence, I care that they develop the skills to provide for themselves and their families, contribute something meaningful, and hopefully help the next generation do the same — especially as we become an interplanetary species.

So yes, sometimes tithing means loading up a trailer and heading toward a disaster. Sometimes it means helping a teenager find a pathway out of poverty. And sometimes it means funding a video game engine.

To me, they're different applications of the same principle: take the resources, knowledge, tools, and opportunities you've been given, and put them to work helping other people. Preferably while building some really cool stuff along the way. 😎

text:
Honestly, it would've been much easier to be a political activist group. It would've kept Redot in the spotlight longer and probably would've raised a good amount of funding for the engine.

But that's not what Redot is, and it's not what we stand for.

Redot is apolitical, and no, being apolitical isn't political.

We know it's hard for the younger generations to understand in this highly politicized world we live in, but there was a time when you could be in online spaces focused on a hobby or topic, and people from all over the world would come together and talk about that without bringing in politics. You could make friends with people of vastly different backgrounds and political views through a shared interest.

Most of us are old enough to remember those days. We want to create that kind of place, where the topic of game development transcends the political talk and culture wars that have taken over every other part of the internet.

As for the game engine itself, we added a 3D terrain editor, structs, traits, nullable static types, and mode7 in Redot 26.3, which just got its 3rd RC release a couple days ago. Many of those are highly requested features for Godot that they still haven't implemented yet, and we have more things that didn't make the cut for 26.3 that'll be in 26.4.

Biased opinion, but we recommend trying out Redot Engine for yourself. Let us know if you run into any bugs or issues that need to be addressed before the stable release.

text: Today, we remember Saint Francis Borgia, a man who had just about everything the world could offer and walked away from it. Born in Spain in 1510, he belonged to the powerful Borgia family. His great-grandfather was Pope Alexander VI, and his mother’s family connected him to Spanish royalty. He served Emperor Charles V, married Eleanor de Castro, raised eight children, and became Duke of Gandía. He enjoyed music, hunting, and privilege. In 1539, he accompanied the body of Empress Isabella to Granada for burial. Tradition tells us that when her coffin was opened, the sight of her remains deeply disturbed him. The woman he had known in all her splendor was gone. He reportedly resolved never again to serve a master who could die. After his wife Eleanor died in 1546, Francis began preparing for a different life. He made private Jesuit vows while providing for his children, then surrendered his title. In 1551, the former duke was ordained a priest. People once bowed when he entered a room. Now he preached the Gospel in village squares. In 1565, he became the third Superior General of the Jesuits. He helped establish colleges and sent missionaries to Mexico, Peru, and Florida. There’s something about his story that makes me uncomfortable in a good way. How much of my life is spent protecting things I can’t keep? My reputation, my position, my possessions, my carefully made plans? None is necessarily bad. But how easily they become more important than they should. Francis couldn’t change the Borgia name he inherited, with all its troubled history. He could decide what kind of man would carry that name forward. We may never surrender a fortune or a title, but every day we can put Christ ahead of our pride, our ambitions, and our need to control everything. Francis Borgia discovered that the only Master worth giving everything to is the One who conquered death. What am I holding on to that keeps me from following Him more faithfully? Saint Francis Borgia, pray for us! #SaintFrancisBorgia #StFrancisBorgia #SaintOfTheDay #CatholicX

text:
A rare and powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck the southern coast of Panama on Friday afternoon, triggering widespread panic, collapsing localized structures across central provinces, and prompting temporary tsunami warnings across Central and South America. Despite severe structural damage to several prominent commercial, historic, and tourist properties, early assessments indicate the country managed to escape a major humanitarian catastrophe, with no confirmed fatalities reported by authorities.

According to data compiled by the U.S. Geological Survey, the main tremor struck at 12:56 p.m. local time at a relatively shallow depth of 12.6 kilometers. The epicenter was located approximately 10 kilometers southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba in the south-central province of Herrera, roughly 200 kilometers from the capital. The sheer energy of the quake affected an estimated 4.6 million people who felt moderate to severe shaking. Vibrations traveled down the Central American isthmus, and tremors were felt as far away as neighboring Colombia. Within hours of the main shock, the region was rattled by more than 40 aftershocks, including a significant magnitude 6.6 secondary quake that sent newly evacuated citizens fleeing back into open streets.

The strongest localized impacts emerged from the central provinces of Coclé, Los Santos, and Herrera. In the city of Penonomé, positioned halfway between the epicenter and the capital, scenes of destruction unfolded as a multi-story hotel building completely collapsed, crushing parked cars below. Dramatic citizen-recorded videos surfaced online showing frantic individuals shouting into the dusty rubble to search for potential survivors. Significant concern also spread rapidly online as footage from the popular Royal Decameron Panama resort property showed collapsed wall segments, severe structural breaches, and debris scattered extensively across the beachfront grounds. The town of Penonomé also witnessed the partial destruction of a 400-year-old parish cathedral, whose historic bell tower crumbled during the initial shaking.

In Panama City, the earthquake triggered immediate automated and manual security protocols. Tens of thousands of workers evacuated skyscrapers in the upscale downtown financial hub. Because elevators were shut down and structural safety inspections were initiated, massive crowds poured into the avenues. The sudden influx, combined with malfunctioning traffic signals, completely gridlocked the capital's transit system. Logistical disruptions also hit critical public services, and Panama’s national water and sewage institute reported operational shutdowns across multiple water treatment plants due to widespread electricity blackouts caused by downing power grids.

Despite the localized damage, Panama's primary economic engines proved highly resilient. The engineering marvel of the Panama Canal reported entirely normal operations. Though dramatic footage surfaced showing the support cables of the canal's famous Centennial Bridge vibrating violently during the tremor, structural engineers confirmed that the vital shipping lane suffered no operational setbacks. Tocumen International Airport temporarily suspended all inbound and outbound flights as a precaution, but after runway inspections returned clear, the civil aviation authority quickly lifted the restriction and normal flight paths resumed later in the day. The massive Cobre Panama copper mine also reported no structural compromises and continued normal operations.

text:
I would say this is a prelude to the extradition and show trial at the ICC of Trump or Netanyahu. Many people mistakenly believe the ICC upholds the highest standards of justice. However, in reality, the appointments are political and often come from countries with appalling human rights records. The political prosecution of Rodrigo Duterte, the former President of the Philippines, exposes the corruption at the court's heart. Widely respected and admired in the Philippines, with an 80% approval rating, Duterte was effectively kidnapped and deported by political opponent President Bongbong Marcos. This is despite the Philippines being a democracy with a functioning judicial system and a Supreme Court based on the American Constitution. The ICC chose to bypass the national justice system in favour of its own politically motivated process.

The ICC accepted substantial funding from his bitter domestic rival, President Bongbong Marcos, who wants to destroy him. The Philippines maintained courts, police records, and a Supreme Court throughout the period, yet the ICC meant his political rival could bypass the domestic justice system.

Once that precedent is set, the same logic applies elsewhere: a sitting or former leader can be extracted from a democratic state with operating courts and placed before judges in The Hague whenever domestic politics or international coalitions align against him.

That precedent is directly relevant to Israel and the United States. Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, already face ICC warrants or investigations tied to operations against Hamas and other armed groups. Under the model applied to Duterte, any country that has accepted the Rome Statute can arrest them on those warrants and transfer them, regardless of Israel’s independent judiciary or the ongoing conflict. The same pathway exists for American figures. Future administrations hostile to Donald Trump, Marco Rubio, or ICE agents could cooperate with an ICC process that treats legitimate political disagreements or border-enforcement actions as crimes against humanity.

The court would not need to prove that U.S. courts have collapsed; it would only need to assert that they are “unwilling” to submit to this political prosecution. The result is a global tribunal that can be activated against political opponents of its supporting states while remaining silent toward regimes that never signed the statute or that maintain influence inside the Assembly of States Parties.

The Office of the Prosecutor's personnel history reinforces this concern. Fatou Bensouda, who served as the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court from 2012 to 2021, passionately pursued a preliminary examination and ultimately authorised an investigation into alleged crimes associated with Rodrigo Duterte. Before her significant ICC role, she was the Attorney General and Minister of Justice in The Gambia from 1998 to 2000. This period was under Yahya Jammeh, a leader whose administration has been widely recognised for its authoritarian and oppressive practices, including the notorious “Junglers” death squad. Jammeh's reign was marked by severe human rights violations, such as extrajudicial killings, press suppression, torture, and the stifling of political dissent, leading to widespread criticism from human rights groups. As Attorney General, Bensouda served as the Government's principal legal adviser, was a Cabinet member, and acted as a political appointee of the President. This role typically overlapped with the Minister of Justice, placing her in the executive branch and aligning her with the government's legislative initiatives.

A coalition of African states supported her election; critics have long argued that the selection process privileged regional political bargains over demonstrated independence from abusive governments. The same structural dynamic would govern any case against an Israeli prime minister or an American politician: the Assembly's political preferences, not an abstract commitment to impartial evidence, would shape prosecutorial leadership and the pool of cooperating states.

Her successor, Karim Khan, was barred from participating in the case against Rodrigo Duterte at the International Criminal Court because of his prior involvement before becoming Prosecutor and allegations of rape. Conflict of interest: Before his appointment as ICC Prosecutor in 2021, Khan practised law privately. During that time, he assisted in preparing and submitting materials to the ICC on behalf of victims relating to alleged crimes committed during Duterte’s “war on drugs.” Appeals judges later found a reasonable appearance of bias and disqualified him from the proceedings. The underlying investigation therefore advanced under a prosecutor who had previously advocated for the very victims whose accounts formed the core of the case, while separate allegations of sexual misconduct against him led to a leave of absence.

The smearing of Duterte was organised by Maria Ressa, a convicted fraudster and libeller with strong connections to Hilary Clinton. Maria Ressa set up a news organisation, Rappler, that planted stories taken up by left-leaning MSM like The Guardian, The Washington Post, CNN and The Sydney Herald. These would then repeat these unproven allegations as proof that the violence occurred. This is bootstrapping, where weak, spurious allegations are repeated and layered on top of one another to create the impression of substantive evidence. Yet this formed the basis of the ICC prosecution.  Maria Ressa was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
Now Navi Pillay fabricated accusations against Israel that ICC prosecutor Karim Khan used to build a case against the country. The Nobel committee is rewarding someone who helped legitimise antisemitism and injustice.

A prosecution built in this manner—prior advocacy, delayed disclosure, and external scandals—offers little reassurance that the same office would handle evidence from Hamas-affiliated witnesses, Palestinian Authority officials, or other hostile actors with greater rigour when the target is an Israeli or American figure.

The evidentiary foundation itself is thin by ordinary domestic standards. The Philippines maintains a national police force, forensic capacity, and court records. Yet the ICC case relies heavily on witness accounts, some from murderers granted forms of protection or immunity, rather than contemporaneous forensic reconstruction or comprehensive police files that would be expected if tens of thousands of bodies had been systematically processed.
The ICC ignored clear evidence of Duterte's active call for lawful enforcement and the offers of amnesty and rehabilitation he offered. Instead, it used assassinations by drug cartels as evidence of police brutality. It selectively edited speeches from Duterte.

My wife’s family in one ordinary barangay in Camarines Sur reported that the nightmare of open drug activity and nighttime disorder stopped after the campaign began, which was enthusiastically supported by the Filipino public; some users accepted rehabilitation, others were arrested and prosecuted through ordinary courts. No mass disappearances were observed by residents who knew the local operators. The vast majority of Filipinos reject the ridiculous assertion that tens of thousands were systematically murdered, as in Argentina, as an absurd accusation and lie.

In Argentina, thousands of relatives campaigned for justice, and their names were well known in their communities. The people called for justice and showed pictures of the thousands of people killed. Now, in complete contrast, such protests and demonstrations of loss are absent in the Philippines. In fact, some of the murder victims are alive.

If someone went missing and were murdered in the Philippines, their friends, relatives and work colleagues would know, and for each victim, that’s hundreds of people who knew about the incident. So if this happened 20-30,000 times, every barangay would be scarred by this brutality. There would be thousands of police records. We have films and photos from Argentina in the 1970s, long before smartphones, that everyone in the Philippines now has. Such a scale of police brutality would be impossible to hide with new technology. Simply put, the evidence of the crimes the ICC is prosecuting does not exist. The International Criminal Court gives these spurious allegations credence for political and financial reasons.

.

Duterte’s relationship with Israel also offers another contrast. He publicly preferred Israeli weapons because they arrived with fewer political conditions than equipment from other suppliers, thanked Israeli leaders for equipment that shortened the Islamic terrorist Marawi siege, and noted the Philippines’ 1947 vote supporting Israel’s creation. He also praised the treatment of roughly 28,000 Filipino caregivers in Israel as better than conditions in several other Middle Eastern states and signed a labour agreement covering them.
My wife, a missionary and midwife, knows many Filipino caregivers who have worked in Israel, and they appreciate the immense kindness and generosity Israelis show them. She contrasts this with the arrogance and mistreatment of Filipinos in Muslim countries.

The picture of a young Filipino caregiver and her elderly dying Jewish lady minutes before they were butchered by arrogant Hamas thugs summed up the evil brutality of Oct 7. Of course this act of brutality was ignored by the pro-Palestinian privileged and entitled students at Western universities who share the same contempt for the poor that Hamas do.

At the detention facility in The Hague, supporters have repeatedly gathered and lined the surrounding street with thousands of flowers and messages on his birthdays. The displays reflect sustained domestic and overseas support that has not evaporated under the weight of the charges, as they know they are false and the trial is politically motivated. It undercuts any narrative that presents Duterte as an indiscriminate enemy of the very people the ICC claims to protect.

The ICC has shown itself ill-equipped to answer with greater independence than the national courts it displaced.

The precedent now exists: a democratic state with functioning institutions can be bypassed, its elected leader extracted, and the prosecution led by officials whose prior service or advocacy raises structural doubts about impartiality. The same mechanism is available for Netanyahu, for Trump, for Rubio, or for ICE agents the moment a sufficient coalition of states decides the political moment has arrived.

text:
🌍 GLOBAL MARKET RECAP — OCTOBER 10, 2026
Weekend Edition | Updated around 09:35 CEST
Traditional Markets: Friday Close | Crypto: Saturday Morning

1️⃣ GLOBAL EQUITIES — WALL STREET RECOVERS, BUT THE UNDERLYING DIVIDE REMAINS
Wall Street ended Friday on a constructive note, with the S&P 500 rising 0.59% to 7,811.54, the Dow gaining 0.83% and the Nasdaq advancing 0.64%, recovering from Thursday's technology-led selloff. The weekly picture was also positive, with the S&P 500 gaining approximately 1.15%, although smaller companies remained comparatively weak. That divergence deserves attention because investors are still favouring businesses capable of sustaining margins, generating cash flow and financing growth without excessive dependence on borrowing. European equities also benefited from easing sovereign yields and an improvement in geopolitical sentiment, while individual technology names remained sensitive to concerns about AI valuations. The important conclusion is that equity resilience remains real, but investors are becoming more discriminating. A market can trade near record highs while significant parts of the economy struggle with financing costs, weak consumption and deteriorating confidence. The next earnings season will determine whether corporate profitability can continue justifying this divergence.

2️⃣ U.S. MACRO — CONSUMERS ARE SENDING A VERY DIFFERENT SIGNAL FROM WALL STREET
The latest University of Michigan survey introduces one of the most important developments of the week. Preliminary October consumer sentiment fell to 46.3 from 48.1 in September, while the assessment of current economic conditions declined sharply to 44.7. More concerning for monetary policy, one-year inflation expectations increased to 4.7% and longer-term expectations reached 3.5%, suggesting households are becoming increasingly uncomfortable with the persistence of elevated prices. This follows September's weak employment report, which showed only 29,000 new jobs and unemployment at 4.2%. Taken together, these indicators reveal an economy where financial-market strength is not translating evenly into household confidence. Higher-income consumers may continue spending, supported by financial assets, while lower-income households face expensive credit, energy bills and weaker employment opportunities. This is not sufficient evidence to declare a recession, but it increases the importance of next week's inflation data and changes the quality of the growth story.

3️⃣ BONDS & FED — TREASURY YIELDS HAVE EASED, BUT CAPITAL REMAINS EXPENSIVE
The U.S. 10-year Treasury finished Friday around 5.243%, while the 2-year ended near 4.789%, following a week in which global bond markets experienced exceptional volatility. Strong demand for the week's Treasury auctions helped restore confidence, particularly after the successful placement of long-duration government debt, but the broader structural pressures remain unresolved. Government borrowing requirements, persistent inflation risk, mortgage-market hedging and the increasing volume of corporate borrowing linked to AI infrastructure are creating competing demands for capital. Markets assign a relatively low probability to another Fed hike in October, while still considering additional tightening later in the year substantially more likely. The critical question is therefore no longer limited to what the Federal Reserve will decide at its next meeting. Investors must also assess how much additional compensation they will demand for holding long-term government debt. The approximately $153.8 billion entering global money-market funds during the latest reporting week illustrates how attractive liquidity has become in this environment.

4️⃣ EUROPE & FX — TEMPORARY RELIEF DOES NOT RESOLVE THE FISCAL PROBLEM
European equities rebounded on Friday, with the STOXX 600 gaining approximately 1%, supported by lower bond yields and the early decline in oil prices. The euro recovered toward $1.123 during the session, although it remained under pressure after several consecutive weeks of losses against the dollar. France continues to represent the most visible source of European sovereign concern, as investors question the political ability to deliver credible fiscal consolidation while supporting an already fragile economic recovery. Meanwhile, the sector rotation has become increasingly significant: European telecommunications shares fell sharply after SpaceX's U.S. spectrum acquisition intensified competitive concerns, while automakers benefited from improving trade prospects with China. The lesson is that European markets are being influenced simultaneously by monetary conditions, fiscal credibility, industrial policy and technological competition. Lower Treasury yields offer welcome short-term relief, but Europe still needs a sustainable solution to the combination of expensive energy, weak domestic demand and growing sovereign refinancing requirements.

5️⃣ ASIA — TECHNOLOGICAL STRENGTH IS COLLIDING WITH DOMESTIC VULNERABILITIES
Asian markets ended the week unevenly, with Japan's Nikkei retreating approximately 1.1%, while Hong Kong performed more strongly and mainland Chinese equities registered modest gains after the holiday period. The region continues to benefit from global semiconductor investment and demand for artificial-intelligence infrastructure, but these advantages are distributed very unevenly. Japan remains sensitive to the weak yen, imported energy prices and the prospect of further Bank of Japan tightening, while India has already raised its policy rate to 5.5% as authorities confront inflationary pressure. China faces a different challenge, with export-oriented technology and manufacturing demand providing support even as domestic consumption and the property sector remain structurally weak. This explains why treating Asia as a single market is becoming increasingly misleading. Companies integrated into global AI supply chains may enjoy exceptional order visibility, while domestic sectors face higher financing costs and weak household demand. Next week's Chinese trade figures will offer another important test of this divergence.

6️⃣ OIL, GOLD & COMMODITIES — THE FRIDAY SETTLEMENT CHANGES THE NARRATIVE
Energy markets delivered one of Friday's most important reversals. Brent initially retreated following encouraging U.S.–Iran diplomatic signals, but ultimately settled at $104.72 per barrel, while WTI closed at $91.85. The late recovery was driven partly by Hurricane Isaias, which forced operators to suspend more than 70% of U.S. Gulf of Mexico offshore oil production, representing approximately 1.3 million barrels per day. At the same time, Washington announced an agreement involving additional Russian diesel supplies, temporarily easing certain restrictions in an attempt to reduce refined-fuel prices. These developments underline why crude supply, refining capacity and fuel logistics must be analysed separately. Gold also recovered, with spot bullion reaching approximately $4,194 late Friday, supported by bargain buying and some relief in yields and the dollar. The broader lesson is that energy inflation remains vulnerable to physical disruptions even when diplomatic developments temporarily improve sentiment.

7️⃣ GEOPOLITICS — ENERGY DIPLOMACY IS BECOMING AN INSTRUMENT OF ECONOMIC POLICY
The geopolitical picture has become more complicated following two significant developments. Washington indicated that another military attack against Iran would not take place before the November 3 midterm elections, reducing immediate fears of escalation without establishing a comprehensive peace agreement or normalising shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Separately, President Trump announced arrangements for Russia to supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to U.S. and international markets, accompanied by temporary sanctions relief. The decision generated criticism from Ukraine and American lawmakers because measures intended to reduce domestic energy inflation may simultaneously weaken economic pressure on Moscow. This illustrates how energy security, electoral considerations, sanctions policy and military diplomacy are becoming increasingly interconnected. For financial markets, these developments should be evaluated through their actual impact on maritime traffic, refined-product availability, insurance costs and inflation expectations rather than political statements alone. A temporary reduction in escalation risk is constructive, but the physical energy system remains vulnerable.

8️⃣ ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE — REAL DEMAND, GREATER SCRUTINY OF FINANCIAL RETURNS
AI delivered two apparently contradictory signals this week, and both deserve attention. The debate surrounding OpenAI's annualised revenue intensified after reporting highlighted approximately $50 billion in net revenue compared with earlier references to figures around $70 billion. Much of the apparent discrepancy reflects differences in accounting and presentation, particularly the treatment of revenues shared with infrastructure and distribution partners, rather than proof of a sudden collapse in customer demand. Nevertheless, investors are demanding greater transparency as AI infrastructure commitments become increasingly expensive. Nvidia-backed Australian data-centre developer Firmus also abandoned its planned IPO amid valuation concerns, reinforcing the importance of financial discipline. On the other side of the equation, optical-networking specialist Lumentum reported exceptionally strong demand, with certain AI-related components effectively sold out into early 2029. The underlying technology cycle remains powerful, but markets are beginning to separate genuine demand, accounting methodology, infrastructure bottlenecks and the eventual return on invested capital.

9️⃣ CRYPTO — BITCOIN HOLDS ABOVE $82K, BUT THE BREAKOUT REMAINS UNCONFIRMED
Saturday-morning quotations place Bitcoin around $82.6K–82.7K, Ethereum near $2.49K and Solana around $109–110. These levels reflect a market attempting to stabilise after a difficult week in which Bitcoin retreated from the $86K–87K region toward $80K before recovering some ground. The relative strength of Wall Street compared with digital assets suggests that crypto remains particularly sensitive to liquidity conditions, leverage and the opportunity cost created by high Treasury yields. From a technical perspective, the $80K area remains the immediate structural reference, while a recovery above $83K–85K would improve the short-term configuration. The $87.4K–90K region remains the broader resistance zone requiring meaningful confirmation. For a long-term BTC, ETH and SOL accumulation strategy, short-term volatility should be assessed independently from the investment thesis and managed through disciplined allocation. For tactical trading, the priority remains confirmation, position sizing and avoiding excessive leverage before the market demonstrates renewed demand.

🔟 MARKET STRUCTURE — THE NEXT WEEK COULD REDEFINE THE BALANCE BETWEEN GROWTH AND INFLATION
The global financial system is currently being influenced by three overlapping forces: geopolitical uncertainty is keeping energy prices elevated, governments must refinance increasingly expensive debt, and the AI investment cycle requires enormous amounts of additional capital. Friday's equity recovery demonstrates that markets still expect economic resilience and corporate profitability, but the latest consumer-confidence figures show how uneven that resilience has become. The next critical catalyst is the September U.S. CPI release scheduled for October 14, followed by the opening of the major-bank earnings season and the IMF–World Bank meetings in Bangkok. Investors will be looking for confirmation that inflation can moderate without forcing the Fed into further aggressive tightening, while bank results will reveal how higher rates are affecting credit, deposits and profitability. The constructive scenario requires stabilising energy prices, sustained Treasury demand and earnings that justify current valuations. The negative scenario would involve another energy shock, renewed upward pressure on long-term yields or evidence that AI capital expenditure is expanding faster than the returns needed to support it. I continue to monitor the U.S. 10-year around 5.20% and 5.35%, Brent around $100–105 and Bitcoin around $80K and $85K. The defining question for the next market phase is whether economic growth can remain resilient while the price of capital stays structurally elevated.

text:
Ukraine is not hitting Russian refineries for fun. It is hitting them because those plants turn crude into diesel, jet fuel, and gasoline that keep Russian tanks, trucks, aircraft, and occupation logistics running.

A country that launched a full-scale war of aggression does not get a protected energy sector. Under the law of armed conflict, objects that make an effective contribution to military action and whose destruction offers a definite military advantage are military objectives. Refineries feeding the Russian war machine meet that test.

Russia has spent years striking Ukrainian power plants, substations, dams, ports, and heating systems in winter. Moscow does not get to demand immunity for its own fuel system while it tries to freeze and black out Ukrainian cities.

Diesel prices are a real political problem. They are not a legal veto. If higher pump prices were enough to outlaw strikes on an aggressor’s war fuel, every defender would have to fight with one hand tied so distant markets stayed comfortable.

Trump can ask Kyiv to spare refineries. That is a policy preference about inflation and talks. It is not a finding that the targets are illegitimate.

To the people of Ukraine, striking the oil refineries fueling the war against their country is a matter of national survival. For Washington, the political concern is whether those strikes will drive up diesel prices in the United States ahead of the midterms. Those priorities are not morally equivalent.

Zelensky’s job is to degrade Russia’s ability to keep killing Ukrainians, not to manage global product balances for Washington.

If the United States wants those strikes to stop, the serious path is a real energy-for-energy halt: Russia stops hitting Ukrainian infrastructure, Ukraine pauses refinery strikes, with verification. Begging only Ukraine to stand down while Russia keeps firing is not neutrality. It is asking the victim to subsidize the invader’s fuel supply.

Ukraine has the right to hit the refineries that power the army occupying its land. That right does not disappear because diesel is expensive.
